nytimes.com.title: Suspect in Mass Shooting in Krakow, Poland, Dies in Hospital. Here’s What to Know.
nytimes.com.text:
A gunman fatally shot six people on Saturday in the medieval heart of Krakow, Poland’s second-biggest city. Officials said the gunman was believed to be a 24-year-old Polish man, who was shot by the police and remains in the hospital.
On Sunday, the police said officers had found the bodies of the suspect’s parents and sister at his home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a town between Krakow and Warsaw, the capital.
The motive for the shootings remains unclear. On Sunday, the Krakow branch of Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation and described the mass shooting in center of the city as an “act constituting a terrorist offense.”
What happened?
Just after 3 p.m. on Saturday, shots were heard across the market square in Krakow’s Old Town, the police said.
The gunman fired “at random people” from a car he had driven into the square, police said. The square, Rynek Glowny, is one of Poland’s most-visited tourist destinations. On Saturday afternoon, it was busy.

nytimes.com.title: Why Winning Big Matters
nytimes.com.text:
Before the U.S. midterms last week, one big question was whether Donald Trump would contest the election results.
There were certainly reasons to wonder: Trump has never publicly conceded his 2020 loss to Joe Biden. And in the run-up to the 2026 midterms, he tried to interfere with the process to tilt it in favor of Republicans.
But on election night, amid a dramatic wipeout, he accepted the results readily. Today I write about why that might be — and what it can tell us about the conditions under which leaders with authoritarian tendencies accept election results, even when they lose.
Big victories, ready concessions
Hungary, Serbia, and now, the United States. This year, in a string of elections, voters unexpectedly rebuked nationalist populist leaders and their movements.
For many voters there was a fear hanging over all of these ballots: Had these leaders tilted the playing field so much that they could not be defeated? And if they lost, would they accept the results?

nytimes.com.title: Targeted by U.S., Armed Group Strikes Back in Colombia
nytimes.com.text:
A decades-old rebel group launched a deadly attack on a military base in Colombia on Saturday, killing at least three soldiers and injuring more than a dozen, Colombian officials said.
The attack, carried out by explosives-laden drones, was the largest retaliatory strike against Colombian forces since the country’s new president took office in August and declared an all-out offensive on trafficking groups, experts said.
Officials blamed the National Liberation Army, better known by its initials in Spanish, ELN, for the attack, which took place in Santa Rosa del Sur, a town around 100 miles from the Venezuelan border in northern Colombia.
The United States has been helping Colombia and Venezuela target the ELN. On Oct. 30, U.S. forces assisted the Venezuelan Army in a drone attack on the group in Venezuela, providing intelligence and the drones.
The ELN is Colombia’s oldest surviving leftist rebel group and a known cocaine trafficker that controls territory in both Colombia and Venezuela.
Colombia’s president, Abelardo De La Espriella, denounced the attack on the military base, which came the day after authorities arrested an ELN leader expert in illicit finances, known as Carrito, in the area. The president pledged to continue hunting the traffickers.

nytimes.com.title: Germans Miss Merkel, Their Old Chancellor, Though They Dislike Her Policies
nytimes.com.text:
The painting’s subject looks out of place on the museum wall, standing in a bright blue blazer, posing stiffly, her fingers perched tent-like on a table and her lined face unsmiling.
“I think she’s fantastic,” said a museum visitor, Heidi Brandt, gazing up at the painting of Angela Merkel.
Germans are experiencing a strange sort of nostalgia for Ms. Merkel, their former chancellor. At a time of political upheaval, polls show voters would rather see Ms. Merkel steering the country than the current chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Both are from the center-right Christian Democratic party.
After 16 years in power, Ms. Merkel left office in 2021 and her official portrait went on display in late summer at the Bode Museum in Berlin. Daily visits to the museum, which is usually not a top tourist draw, have risen by 80 percent since the exhibit opened. The rush was large enough to cause museum officials to extend the portrait’s stay by several months, through the end of the year.
Mr. Merz’s approval rating stands at 11 percent, said Peter Matuschek, who leads the German polling firm Forsa. Ms. Merkel left office with a rating near 75 percent, crossing party lines.
“People have an overall impression of her as a chancellor who seemed to hold the country together,” Mr. Matuschek said.

nytimes.com.title: Polluted Delhi Tries ‘Green’ Fireworks to Clear the Air at Diwali
nytimes.com.text:
Nothing says it’s time for Diwali like the riot of colors that suddenly appears everywhere — red saris, gold kurtas, garlands of bright orange marigolds. But there’s another color that’s now compulsory in India’s capital: green.
Green, as in the environmentally friendlier fireworks that the Supreme Court of India has said are the only type that can be set off this Diwali weekend. Fireworks are otherwise banned to try to avoid contributing to the toxic haze of dust, vehicle exhaust and smoke from faraway crop fires that envelops New Delhi around this time of year.
The court ruled last week that fireworks — a staple of Diwali celebrations across the country — could be used in the capital region for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday, as long as they were of the “green” variety manufactured to burn faster and emit fewer harmful chemicals.
The court cited Diwali’s “religious, social, psychological and emotional connotation” that fostered “a positive atmosphere of hope, welfare and prosperity.” Since ancient times, the court observed, Hindus had lit fires on the holiday, known as the festival of lights, first with lamps and later with explosives once gunpowder was invented.
After Sunday, the actual day of Diwali, the full ban on the sale and use of all fireworks, implemented by the Delhi government in 2024, goes back into effect.
But the court’s attempt to balance public health and religious expression left some environmental activists incredulous.

nytimes.com.title: In Argentina, Pope Leo Tells President Milei Economy Must Serve the Needy
nytimes.com.text:
The Catholic priests were reciting the Lord’s Prayer last May during an anti-government protest when clashes broke out with the police. As one cleric tried to reach a fellow priest dragged behind the armored police cordon, an officer in riot gear grabbed his white tunic.
“This government is heartless,” the priest, Jorge Romero, said in a later interview. “We have to fight,” said the other, Francisco Olveira, known as Paco.
The clash between the police and activist clergymen outside Argentina’s Congress in Buenos Aires was a violent flashpoint in prolonged tensions between President Javier Milei and much of the country’s Roman Catholic Church.
Pope Leo landed in Argentina on Sunday as part of a 12-day South American tour that includes Uruguay and Peru. The Argentina visit places him at the center of that uneasy standoff with Mr. Milei, a libertarian economist who has repeatedly attacked the concepts of social justice to which much of the country’s Catholic clergy is deeply committed.
The pontiff met with Mr. Milei at the presidential palace in the afternoon, then addressed him along with diplomats and civic leaders in an auditorium. He implored them to “acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community.”
He reminded them to serve the needs of the unemployed, retirees and workers who struggle to make ends meet saying, “The economy must be at the service of the person, not the person in the service of the economy.” The auditorium exploded repeatedly in applause.

nytimes.com.title: Trains Collide Near Cairo, Killing 4
nytimes.com.text:
At least seven people were killed and 125 injured on Sunday when two passenger trains crashed south of Cairo, the authorities said, renewing scrutiny of a beleaguered rail system that the Egyptian government has spent billions of dollars trying to modernize.
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of Egypt, who has made infrastructure spending a centerpiece of his rule, said he had ordered an investigation into the deadly crash. He added that anyone found negligent should be held accountable.
“I am closely following the aftermath of the train collision,” he said in a statement on social media, offering his “sincere condolences” to the families of those killed.
The crash, which derailed several cars, occurred between Kafr Ammar and al-Riqqa in the al-Ayyat district when one train hit the rear of the other, according to Egypt’s transport ministry. Emergency crews were working to clear the wreckage, according to the ministry, and dozens of ambulances were sent to the site to transport the injured.
The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, according to a statement from the Ministry of Health; more than 70 of the injured have since been released. Many suffered bruising and abrasions, while others were being treated for various fractures, the ministry said, expressing its condolences to the families of the victims who lost their lives and wishing a speedy recovery to the injured.
Egypt’s rail network has long struggled with aging infrastructure and weak oversight. The deadly collision was the latest in a string of railway disasters in al-Ayyat, a largely rural district south of Cairo, the capital.
More than 350 people were killed in al-Ayyat in 2002 — Egypt’s deadliest rail disaster — when fire tore through an overcrowded train carrying passengers south for Eid al-Adha, one of the most important holidays in the Muslim calendar.
In 2009, a train struck the rear of a stalled train there, killing at least 25 people. Five more were killed in a derailment in al-Ayyat in 2016. In September of this year, two freight trains collided, injuring two crew members.
Egypt operates one of the world’s oldest rail systems, carrying between 1.1 million and 1.2 million passengers daily, according to state figures. For millions of Egyptians, rail travel provides an essential and relatively inexpensive link to the capital.

nytimes.com.title: Reeling From Rare Mass Shooting, Poles Ask What Set Off Young Suspect
nytimes.com.text:
He lived with his parents on the top floor of a three-story apartment building painted a sunny yellow, but he nearly always dressed in black. He attended sedate family events like christenings but was fascinated by guns and the history of World War II.
A day after the authorities said a 24-year-old man had killed his sister and parents at their home and then shot dead six people in the central square of Krakow, neighbors and relatives in the gritty former steel town where the family lived were struggling to piece together what had happened. What, they asked, might have pushed an often sullen but seemingly unaggressive young man with no criminal record to mass murder?
“My legs are still shaking from shock,” said Ryszard Piasecki, who is related by marriage to the suspect’s slain mother, Renata. “He was a loner and didn’t have a girlfriend or any friends at all. He always wore black — but lots of young people do that.”
The suspect, Michal Oksinski, was a lathe operator. His parents and sister, Magdalena, a third-year student at the Fine Arts Academy in Krakow, were found late Saturday in their apartment in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a Communist-era industrial center now fallen on hard times.
Magdalena, 21, was visiting for the weekend when her brother killed her on Saturday morning, according to investigators.
One Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski resident, Marta Piwowarczyk, said her brother-in-law lived in the same apartment building as the Oksinskis and called her on Saturday to say the police had sealed off the area and that “something terrible seems to have happened.”

nytimes.com.title: Who Is Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s Opposition Leader?
nytimes.com.text:
The clock started ticking on Sunday for Gadi Eisenkot, the leading rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, to form a new government.
After days of consultations, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, presided over a ceremony that officially gave Mr. Eisenkot the mandate to forge a coalition after an inconclusive national election last month. “This is the time to reach out a hand, to do everything for the unity of our people,” Mr. Herzog said.
Mr. Eisenkot vowed to form a government “for all Israelis” and, in a nod to Israel’s fractured electoral landscape, said that it would take “creative and unconventional political steps.”
A soft-spoken former general, Mr. Eisenkot leads Yashar, a center-right party that campaigned on a promise of keeping Israel secure while pivoting away from policies that prompted international anger and led to Israel’s isolation on the world stage.
Mr. Eisenkot, 66, has up to six weeks to build a coalition before the president passes the opportunity to another candidate, most likely Mr. Netanyahu. Here’s what to know about the career general-turned-politician.
What is his background?
Mr. Eisenkot, a married father of five, was born in Tiberias, in the north, to Moroccan immigrants and was raised in Eilat, a working-class city in southern Israel.

nytimes.com.title: More Than 50 Killed in Yemen in One of the Deadliest 24 Hours of the War
nytimes.com.text:
More than 50 people have been killed in Yemen over the past 24 hours, in what appeared to be one of the deadliest stretches since the conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and the government of Yemen backed by Saudi Arabia reignited in recent months.
Houthi officials said airstrikes tore through the village of al-Shariya, in the Bani Hushaysh district east of the capital, Sanaa, on Saturday. Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi-run Health Ministry, said at least 27 people were killed and 30 others wounded, most of them women and children, and blamed Saudi warplanes. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to questions about the strikes.
The attack in Sanaa took place a day after strikes on a crowded market in Taiz Province killed at least 30 people, according to a Houthi-run news agency. The warring parties traded blame for the attack. The authorities in government-held Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, said the Houthis were responsible, but officials for the Iran-backed group blamed Saudi Arabia.
The past few days’ high toll underscores the growing ferocity of the war since it resumed in August. Almost 1,800 people had been killed by the end of October and more than 300,000 people had been displaced, the World Health Organization said last week. Aid agencies have warned that hospitals in Yemen are running short of medical supplies.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that the fighting is returning to the levels seen a decade ago, before a cease-fire was signed in 2022. A Saudi-led coalition waged a yearslong air campaign against the Houthis after the group seized control of Sanaa and ousted the government in 2014. The conflict contributed to hundreds of thousands of deaths from violence, hunger and disease, causing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

cnn.com.title: How the midterms shook up Senate delegations for 2027
cnn.com.text: Democrats’ red-state dreams came true in the midterm elections. What feels like a watershed moment for those normally red states also reverses a recent trend of polarization on Capitol Hill. Heading into Election Day, there were only four split Senate delegations — meaning states represented by senators from more than one party. That was the fewest since the nationwide election of senators began with the 1914 election after the ratification of the 17th amendment, according to a 2021 analysis by Pew. In January, there will be at least 10 such delegations; there could be up to 12 if Democratic candidates win unresolved races in Mississippi and Alaska. It’s a return to the historical norm. The split delegations will include Vermont, where Sen. Bernie Sanders is technically independent, but sides with Democrats for procedural matters. Also on the list will be Maine, where Democrat Troy Jackson will join the independent Sen. Angus King, who, like Sanders, caucuses with Democrats. The changing political map is also a good reminder that American politics are more elastic than many people realize. Kansas on Tuesday elected a Democrat to the US Senate for the first time since the Great Depression. But that 94-year streak, now broken, was unlike anything else in US politics. In fact, since Kansas became a state in 1861, Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton will be only the fourth Democrat to represent it in Senate history. It’s a remarkable statistic especially because the two parties have evolved so much during that time. Hamilton won Kansas in part by promising to work across the aisle and arguing that his state would be better served having lawmakers from both parties. For Texas and Mississippi, the last Democrats were elected in the 1980s. They would join, if Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom wins, the majority of states that have been represented by a senator from both major parties within the past 25 years. The longest one-party streaks are now in Hawaii, Wyoming and Utah No Republican has been elected to represent the islands since 1970. That Republican, Hiram Fong, was one of Hawaii’s first two senators, elected when Hawaii became a state in 1959. No Democrat has been elected to represent Wyoming or Utah since that same year. The longest streak east of the Mississippi River is in New Jersey, where no Republican has been elected to the US Senate since Clifford Case was elected in 1972, capping a long career on Capitol Hill. A Republican senator, Jeffrey Chiesa, was briefly appointed to serve in 2013. That was the result of the state having a Republican governor, Chris Christie, at the time. Voters can split state and federal offices New Hampshire is represented by two Democratic senators, and that will continue after Rep. Chris Pappas, who won the election there, is sworn in. The last Republican elected as a senator was Kelly Ayotte in 2010. She’s currently the state’s governor, and was elected to a second term on Tuesday. Both Dakotas and Montana were represented by two Democrats within the last 25 years. Now all three states are represented by two Republicans, although this year in Montana, South Dakota and Nebraska it was independents, not Democrats, who mounted the biggest challenge to Republicans. None of them won.

cnn.com.title: Planetary extremes are ‘off the charts’ as world’s biggest climate talks kick off
cnn.com.text: The climate and weather extremes endured by the planet over the course of 2026 will continue into next year, and give “new meaning to off the charts,” according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization, published Monday as the world’s biggest climate talks begin in Turkey. The report, timed to inform discussions at the UN-led COP31 climate conference, highlights a slew of unprecedented climate events and warns worse may be to come as as a super-sized El Niño — the natural climate pattern that typically boosts global temperatures — gains strength. “We are supercharging our weather and El Niño will be a risk multiplier. Heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for,” said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. 🥶 Get your local forecast in the CNN Weather app The analysis, which looks at data from January 2025 to September 2026,  sets out a raft of climate superlatives: “We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” said UN Secretary-General António Guterres. “A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising.” And this year, these costs have been unbearably clear. They can be seen in series of brutal heat waves that roiled Europe this summer, which are estimated to have killed more than 50,000 people, although scientists say even that staggering number is likely an undercount. They are shown in the the rock-ice avalanche that tore through the valleys on the Nepal-China border killing more than 1,300 people, a tragedy scientists say was influenced by climate change and its impact on the ice that acts like glue in the Himalayan peaks. From flooding in Vietnam, to low monsoon rainfall in India, countries across the world have grappled with climate change-driven extremes, damaging food production, eroding livelihoods and increasing poverty. The world cannot expect a reprieve next year, the report cautions. The very strong El Niño we are currently experiencing is expected to unleash more heat and extreme weather well into 2027, which some scientists predict may end up the hottest year on record. The report comes as leaders prepare to make their speeches at the opening of COP31 in Antalya, Turkey. Over the next two weeks, countries will be locked in negotiations focused on how to shift the world away from planet-heating fossil fuels and toward clean energy, as well as who should pay and how much to those countries already facing the catastrophic climate impacts. COP conferences often end up mired in fierce disagreements, with some some countries pushing for ambitious action while others, dominated by the major oil-producing nations, push back. The resulting outcomes are often criticized as weak and ineffectual. Last year’s final agreement didn’t even mention fossil fuels — the main driver of the climate crisis. The UN Secretary-General has urged countries to increase their ambition levels in the face of accelerating climate change. “Leaders must get serious by cutting emissions faster,” Guterres said, “accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need.”

cnn.com.title: Gunman who killed at least 6 in Kraków mass shooting has died in hospital
cnn.com.text: A gunman who killed at least six people during a deadly rampage in the Polish city of Kraków on Saturday has died in hospital, Reuters news agency reported on Monday, citing police. The country was horrified by the rare mass shooting in the historic main square of the city in the country’s south, which prompted national mourning and heightened security, as authorities said the attack was likely driven by far-right ideology. The Polish citizen, in his 20s, was shot and injured by police during the attack before being transported to hospital. There, he underwent multiple surgeries and had been in a critical condition prior to his death. The mass shooting — which authorities said they are investigating as a possible terror attack — has generated a wave of fear in a European nation with exceptionally tight gun laws. Kraków police said the gunman drove into the city’s main market square, typically popular with tourists and locals, and started firing randomly at people, initially from his car, killing four women and two men, on Saturday afternoon. Sixteen others were injured, including two police officers. The alleged attacker was wearing military-style clothing and used “military weapons,” Police Deputy Inspector Katarzyna Cisło told Polish news outlet TVN24. Weapons and ammunition were also found in his vehicle. The bodies of his sister, mother and father were later found at the suspect’s home in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 120 miles northeast of Kraków. Poland’s prosecutor’s office said Sunday that it is “highly likely” the killings were carried out by the same person, but investigations were ongoing. Eleven firearms were recovered from both sites, the prosecutor’s office spokesperson said. Gunman’s clothing examined Little is known about the gunman, who has not been identified by police, and his motive was not immediately clear. But Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said that the shooter was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical views.” Emblems on his clothing were being examined by experts, an interior ministry spokesperson said on Monday. “These patches were associated with various motifs that are currently being analyzed by specialists,” Karolina Galecka told radio TOK FM, Reuters reported. The suspect was a member of a shooting club and appeared to be highly skilled marksman, the club spokesperson Adam Chyb told Reuters on Sunday. Poland, like other European Union countries, has strict rules about acquiring guns and very few people are allowed to own military-style weapons or carry guns in public. About 411,000 people have gun permits in the country, which has a population of more than 37 million, according to the Associated Press. Off-duty surgeons saved lives An off-duty surgeon who rushed to the scene of the shooting to treat victims of the attack, including a police officer, said he had just finished eating lunch with his family when he heard “what sounded like gunshots.” Michal Pedziwiatr described being “in the eye of the storm” as he and a friend – also a surgeon – began providing care to the wounded. Pedziwiatr told a press conference on Sunday that his friend, Mateusz Wierdak, was a “hero” for saving the life of a police officer who subdued the attacker, after he “applied pressure to the bleeding wound without any protective gear or gloves” and “stuffed gauze pads into the chest cavity,” Reuters reported. The two wounded police officers, who Polish Prime ​Minister ‌Donald Tusk praised for also saving “many lives,” underwent surgery and remain in hospital, police said. This is a developing story and will be updated.

cnn.com.title: US and Iran are quietly negotiating as Middle East remains on edge. Here’s what to know
cnn.com.text: US President Donald Trump has offered his clearest indication yet that intensified diplomacy could avert another major round of fighting with Iran, in the wake of his party’s disastrous midterm election results. Trump told CNN on Sunday that renewed US military attacks are “highly unlikely” if Tehran makes progress toward an agreement on its nuclear program and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. He also told CBS’ “60 Minutes” that he was “not looking to” escalate the war. Iran and the United States have quietly been negotiating a sensitive agreement that could avert a return to all-out war and open the door to broader talks. But hopes of a deal are being tempered by Washington, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying Sunday that he “wouldn’t say we’re on the verge of a breakthrough.” Trump has also made clear the military option remains on the table. Both sides and Qatar, which is mediating, have revealed little about the discussions even as diplomatic activity has accelerated since Tuesday’s midterms. What’s changed since the midterms? The Republican losses in the elections have added another dimension to the negotiations, with Vice President JD Vance saying aftewards that the war was among the reasons Republicans lost. Trump told “60 Minutes” that he did not disagree with Vance’s assessment, acknowledging that voters “didn’t like the war.” But he strongly defended the decision to attack Iran, saying that if he had to make the decision again, his answer would be “an emphatic yes.” Iran, meanwhile, has sought to use the election results to press its negotiating position. “American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday. Trump continues to project confidence about the US military position, while Iran has repeatedly threatened to expand the war geographically if it is attacked again. What is being discussed? Both sides have several key demands that are on paper non-starters to the other. Trump seeks to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program, which Tehran sees as a matter of national sovereignty. Publicly, Iran is posturing, insisting it will not negotiate with Washington over the program or reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz unless seven preconditions are met —including ending the war on “all fronts” and lifting a maritime blockade. The specifics are yet to be made public. Hundreds of kilograms of enriched uranium – the material needed to produce a nuclear weapon – remain hidden somewhere in Iran. Tehran has used this stockpile as leverage in its talks with the US. Reports indicate Washington wants the uranium diluted or transferred to another country for safekeeping. It is unclear how far the two sides have progressed on that point. Iran has contended that its nuclear program is for generating energy and not military purposes. For Iran, aside from not ceding ground on its nuclear program or Hormuz, there are key economic goals. As one of the world’s largest oil producers, Iran has found it increasingly difficult to sell crude on global markets under US sanctions. Billions of dollars in Iranian assets held in foreign banks also remain frozen. Washington appears to be weighing relief on these restrictions, a move that could help Tehran ease the severe economic strain on its population amid record inflation. Iran also wants compensation from the US for the killing of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and his top military commanders by the US and Israel at the start of the war in February. Qatar is mediating between the two sides and circulating a framework document that both Washington and Tehran are amending. The process has been underway for weeks, possibly months, but has intensified in recent days amid fears of fresh strikes. Trump is expected to meet Qatari Prime Minster Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al Thani in Washington on Monday. What’s stopping a deal? So far neither side has been willing to budge on its demands. Before leaving Sunday for the Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested the two sides remained far from an agreement. “Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.” After successive rounds of open conflict, Tehran’s trust in Washington has almost vanished. Iran has not forgotten that the conflict began while nuclear talks with the US were underway. Iran is concerned that relinquishing any leverage could invite the US and Israel to strike again, leaving it exposed and without effective negotiating tools. If Iran is attacked after opening the Strait of Hormuz and relinquishing control over the enriched uranium, it would be left even more exposed and in a weaker negotiating position. Trump is balancing his ties with Arab partners and Israel – both of which view the Islamic Republic as a threat – and faces scrutiny if he walks away from the war without a major concession from Iran. Tehran also wants to protect its regional proxies and allies in Lebanon, Iraq and Yemen. Those militias have fought on behalf of the Islamic Republic regionally and are loyal to Tehran, but have come under existential pressure over the past three years. In September, Iran’s ally in Yemen, the Houthi rebels, launched a lighting offensive capturing another key maritime chokepoint on the Red Sea – Bab Al Mandeb – and giving Tehran potential influence over another waterway. The Houthis have since ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia in response to Riyadh giving the Yemeni government military support. The US wants Iran not to have capabilities to build a nuclear weapon, including advanced equipment that could allow it to do so. Iran’s Arab neighbors are divided over any agreement that would hand Tehran too much power and cement its desired hegemony. Iran wants to administer the Strait of Hormuz, the maritime corridor through which wealthy Arab states export most of their oil and gas. Control of the waterway would give Tehran decisive influence over what enters and leaves the region. This too would go against the demands of the US, which wants to see open waterways and would be loath to cement one of Iran’s key gains from the war. So, will war resume? There have been some attacks but both sides have played them down, a sign perhaps that neither wants to derail talks. Some outlets report that talks between the two sides have moved closer to agreement. The New York Times has indicated that Iran is willing to re-engage in nuclear negotiations. There has been no independent confirmation but any concessions from Iran on its nuclear program, or even willingness to discuss the topic, would be considered a breakthrough. Yet, despite reports of progress, the risk of an all-out war remains real. The US still has a vast military presence in the Middle East that could launch a major assault on Trump’s orders. Vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz with oil and gas continue to come under Iranian attack. The US is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear program and has launched a task force aimed at blocking Tehran from using land routes to move advanced weapons and other materials – signs that Washington is intensifying pressure rather than easing it. Meanwhile, Iranian hardliners who believe Tehran has already emerged victorious in its war with the US are seizing on Trump’s midterm losses to demand that he pay a steeper price for an exit from the conflict. Should a deal be reached by the more reformist-minded Iranian leaders involved in talks they could face opposition at home. Over the past weeks, Iranian military commanders have stepped up their warnings claiming Iran possesses weaponry capable of striking more targets and inflicting even greater damage than before. So, even if Trump is willing to reach deal, it is far from clear if Iran is ready to accept.

cnn.com.title: Trump team interprets midterms debacle as a cue to go harder, further, faster
cnn.com.text: It’s as if the midterms never happened. The Trump administration is heading into this week’s impeachment showdown over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth— the first major test of the president’s power after his election debacle — with a clear warning that it plans to use executive authority with even greater force in the new political era. There’s little sense of contrition or acknowledgment that Americans voted to impose restraints on President Donald Trump. The unequivocal White House response was instead represented by the appointment of Stephen Miller, the architect of many of Trump’s most aggressive policies, as White House chief of staff. Attorney General Todd Blanche spelled out the message on CNN on Sunday morning, saying Democrats who plan to employ constitutional prerogatives to investigate the administration should be “worried” after Trump demanded Department of Justice criminal probes into their activity. In dueling interviews on “State of the Union,” the administration and its critics laid down political battle lines for next year. “Before they’re even in power, they’re already talking about investigations and impeachments, with no basis, no facts, just out there running around,” Blanche told CNN’s Dana Bash. “That should be something that President Trump is very concerned about, and certainly I am as well.” But Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, warned the new Democratic Congress would not cow before a “threat” from Blanche. “He’s trying to stop us from doing real oversight. … The Constitution makes it very clear that it’s our job in the Congress to conduct oversight of the executive and the administration,” Garcia said. Hegseth impeachment will showcase GOP anger with Trump But the first confrontation, over a potential House of Representatives vote to impeach Hegseth, will do more to test how the midterm wipeout has hurt Trump’s authority among Republicans than Democrats’ capacity to restrain him. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie plans to bring articles of impeachment against Hegseth this week as the Pentagon chief intensifies a vehement campaign to keep his job despite criticism of his conduct of the Iran war. There are growing suggestions that even many Republicans would like the combative Hegseth gone, especially after Rep. James Comer expressed reservations about him last week. Comer, unlike his fellow Kentuckian Massie, who was beaten by a pro-Trump rival in his primary, remains loyal to the president. The White House is standing by Hegseth, so far. Trump told reporters last week his defense secretary was doing “a very good job.” And Hegseth reacted to Miller’s promotion by portraying him as a fellow fighter against the president’s enemies with a social media post reading “Stand. Fight.” Hegseth’s viability, however, could be undermined by a strong vote against him by GOP members. Those who’ve lost their jobs amid public fury over Iran may have little incentive to stand strong with him and the president. It seems unlikely that there will be the two-thirds majority in the Senate needed to convict and remove Hegseth from office in an impeachment trial. But he’s made few friends in the Senate, and these are volatile political days. The Hegseth impeachment drama will unfold against the last rites of the lame-duck Republican-led Congress, which must pass a funding bill by December 11 to keep the government open. The defense secretary’s controversial presence may also complicate the Senate passage of a critical defense spending bill. Battle lines drawn over Congress vs. White House confrontation In the first days after the Democrats’ midterm rout, Trump seemed subdued. But now it’s clear the White House wants a fight. Asked on Sunday’s edition of CBS’ “60 Minutes” whether he could ever forgive his enemies, Trump answered: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.” On Saturday, Trump complained on Truth Social that Democrats had sent threatening letters to Republicans and donors and ordered the Justice Department to investigate them, while claiming “these extortionists” should be imprisoned. Last week, Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal issued a warning to individuals, companies and government agencies to cooperate with investigations into “cryptocurrency; corruption involving the Trump Administration’s self-enrichment and national security threats; rampant misconduct by federal immigration agents; Big Tech and other corporate enablers; and the Trump Administration’s lawless abuse of power.” Blumenthal said that if the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations did not get responses by January, the new Congress would act. Also last week, Garcia said in a video that “crooks, the con men and the Trump crime family” need to “lawyer up.” Blanche argued that such rhetoric goes too far. “You have an incoming chairman threatening … they’re not even in charge yet — saying, ‘Lawyer up’ to anybody in particular. So, if that doesn’t bother you, if that doesn’t bother your viewers, then we really need to kind of wake up in this country, because it certainly bothers me,” Blanche told CNN. The attorney general said Garcia’s complaints about his own vow to represent officials targeted by congressional investigations showed “a remarkable lack of understanding of how government works.” He added: “I would be very worried if I was a member on that committee.” But Garcia hit back. “Quite frankly, what Todd Blanche is doing right now is a threat,” he said on “State of the Union.” “He is threatening our committee. He’s trying to stop us from doing real oversight,” the California Democrat said of Blanche, arguing that “all he wants to do is protect Donald Trump, is protect Donald Trump’s Cabinet and administration officials.” Democrats have their own risks heading into new era The appearances by Blanche and Garcia gave a preview of Washington next year and the risks both parties are likely to take during Trump’s last two years in office. The administration is implying that any true oversight of the administration is illegitimate; what Trump called “Weaponization and Lawfare” on Truth Social. This strategy was successful when Trump leveraged investigations into his company, his efforts to overturn the 2020 election and his retention of classified material into a narrative of political persecution that unified Republicans and helped him to reclaim the presidency in 2024. It’s not surprising that he’s trying to turn the same trick now, since Blanche, then one of his top personal lawyers, was a chief architect of his legal fight. The Republicans’ midterm election defeat was about many things: the Iran war, the cost of living, soaring gas prices, public distaste with immigration crackdowns, and a sense Trump pursues his own interests over the country’s. But the administration is showing it plans to wring every ounce of power from Trump’s term. Increasingly, top officials are speaking in rather apocalyptic terms. As he professed his “total devotion” and “absolute loyalty” to Trump at Mar-a-Lago on Friday, Miller warned that if it weren’t for the president, “the United States of America would not exist right now.” In his videos fighting for his job, Hegseth pledges to defend the republic against “all enemies, foreign and domestic.” All this implies the administration sees some domestic opponents as bent on destroying the country — which just voted in a democratic election to repudiate its current rulers. Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, who won a stunning upset victory in Kansas, expressed concern about the administration’s response to the elections. He described Miller’s appointment as “almost a doubling down” and told CNN that “people in my state, which is typically a pretty red state, have said, ‘This is not OK. This is not who we are.’” But the aftermath of the elections also underscores the challenges facing the incoming Democratic majority. While Democrats made investigating Trump’s alleged corruption a centerpiece of their campaigns, and therefore have a mandate, voters primarily issued a cry for help with the cost of living. Acting on such concerns will be difficult enough, since Trump is armed with a presidential veto. A bitter climate of investigations could poison any hope of cooperation. Xochitl Hinojosa, a CNN political commentator and former senior Justice Department official, told Bash she is “worried the Democrats will overreach.” Hinojosa added: “I do think that there needs to be some oversight, because there have been no checks on this administration whatsoever. But both parties need to realize that the voters said, ‘We do not want infighting. We do not want Republicans and Democrats going at each other. What we want is people to deliver results.’” Sunday’s fierce political exchanges show how hard that will be.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s regrets on immigration enforcement, and other takeaways from his ‘60 Minutes’ interview
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump offered his most extensive assessment yet of historic Republican losses in an interview with “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday evening, appearing to extend an invitation to Democrats to work together on the contentious issue of immigration. Trump took no personal blame for the wipeout, despite his record unpopularity. He said GOP candidates weren’t able to translate his popularity to their own races. And while he acknowledged areas where his record was unpopular, he made clear he wasn’t in a conciliatory mood on most issues as Democrats prepare to take majorities on Congress. Deportations were ‘too tough’ As he assessed why Republicans fared so poorly in last week’s elections, Trump named Iran and bad messaging as the primary culprits. But he also acknowledged that his administration’s crackdown on immigration that saw thousands of undocumented migrants arrested and deported was unpopular, and in his view went too far. “It was too tough. I think it might be too tough,” Trump said, citing in particular immigrants who have been in the country for ten years or more without committing serious crimes. It was a striking acknowledgement from the president that a topic he ran on in 2024 has, in two years, become politically toxic. Behind the scenes, Trump has expressed misgivings at some of the tactics his administration has employed in rounding up migrants. Still, it’s unclear whether Trump is considering any changes to his immigration agenda, even after conceding it was too hard-line. He just named the architect of the policies, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff. Would rather go to hell than forgive The interview with CBS’ Ross Douthat ended on a revealing back-and-forth over whether Trump could ever forgive his perceived enemies — even ahead of his final judgement before God. “I think they were very bad people, and I dislike — I can use the word hate — I do hate some of my enemies,” Trump said, before concluding: “I probably cannot do that now because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.” The question was prefaced by recounting a moment last year at the funeral for slain activist Charlie Kirk, where his widow, Erika, publicly forgave his alleged assassin. Moments later, Trump appeared onstage to declare: “I hate my opponents, and I don’t want the best for them.” Trump has cultivated a long list of grievances, from Democrats and other officials who led investigations into him during his first term to rival politicians who have opposed his agenda. While he has at moments voiced a desire for conciliation — including last week when he said he wanted to work with newly powerful Democrats — his default has always been to retrench into his perceived injustices. A note for Vance When Vice President JD Vance wrote last week that the Iran war was to blame for the Republican wipeouts, Trump sounded mostly supportive. A few days later, however, he has qualified his response. Now, he says he wishes Vance had been more supportive of the conflict even while assessing its political fallout. “The only thing I wish he would have said there — if he felt it, and you’d have to ask him about that — but if you had it to do again, would you do it? You know, he’s part of a decision-making process. And my answer is an emphatic yes,” Trump said. He said Vance had spoken to him beforehand about the Iran post, but suggested they did not delve into the content of the lengthy essay. “He asked me, ‘What do I think?’ I said, ‘Write what you feel,’” Trump said as he recounted the conversation he had with Vance beforehand. “By the way, what are you going to write?” Hedging on a successor Vance’s post about Iran was widely interpreted in Washington as a way for the vice president to lay down a marker ahead of a potential run for president. In the interview, Trump suggested Vance would not automatically receive his endorsement should he run. Instead, the president mused he may withhold an endorsement altogether. “Probably. Not necessarily,” Trump said when asked about a potential endorsement, later adding, “Maybe I’m better off not getting involved.” Asked who would be on his shortlist other than Vance, Trump touted Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “I think Marco’s great. I mean, he certainly loves it, and he’s doing great. He’s doing a fantastic job. The ones they think about, but there are many others, and I’d rather not mention their names. There’s some senators that are excellent. I know them all. I like them a lot,” Trump said. As he enters the final stretch of his presidency, Trump will have to grapple with a Republican Party that eventually tries to move on. He said in the interview he still believes his endorsement carries significant weight within the GOP. “I think it would play a big role if I did, because my endorsement capacity has been very strong.” Questions on corruption The most combative portion of the interview came as Douthat pressed Trump on his families extensive business interests, including in crypto, that have drawn corruption accusations from Democrats. Trump said in the interview that one of his sons, who he called a “very straight, good guy,” is the one who manages his money and that most of it is “given to the biggest firms on Wall Street to invest.” The president has raked in more than $1 billion from various crypto businesses that he and his sons launched shortly before he was sworn in last year. An investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates acquired nearly half of the Trump family’s cryptocurrency company ahead of Trump’s second inauguration. The president downplayed concerns that countries are trying to buy influence in the White House, saying that “every president has a problem” with outside entities seeking to curry favor with the president. And he insisted he had no role in his family’s moneymaking ventures, despite not having fully divested. “How do you divest from cash? So, I took a lot of heat because I think they traded, like, 50,000 stocks, because that’s what they do. It’s all computer generated. I have no idea what the hell they’re buying,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Joe Biden says cancer will limit him from promoting his upcoming memoir
cnn.com.text: Former President Joe Biden announced Sunday that he “won’t be able to do as many conversations” about his upcoming presidential memoir due to his fight with prostate cancer. “Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves,” he wrote on social media. Biden’s book, titled “Promise Me, America,” is slated for release on November 17. “I hope you’ll read it,” he wrote on social media. “It covers my years as President. The challenges we faced, the decisions I made, and why I made them. It’s about who we are as a nation. What we stand for. And America’s role in the world.” Biden, who turns 84 on November 20, is the oldest living former president. The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May 2025, less than four months after he left the White House. His office said in a statement then that he appeared to have a “more aggressive” form of cancer but that it “appears to be hormone-sensitive which allows for effective management.” The former president’s son, Hunter Biden, told the BBC in August that his father’s cancer had “metastasized into his bones and further.” “It’s really sad to watch,” Hunter Biden said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.”

cnn.com.title: Pope Leo urges President Milei, a Trump ally, to ‘safeguard democracy’ on arrival in Argentina
cnn.com.text: Pope Leo XIV has called on Argentine President Javier Milei and the country’s political leaders to “safeguard democracy” and demonstrate a “careful use of words” during his first speech in Buenos Aires. The American pope arrived in Argentina on Sunday, embarking on a trip that his predecessor, the first Argentine pope, was never able to make. Leo’s highly anticipated papal visit to Argentina began with a private meeting with President Milei shortly after the pope landed. Milei has received strong backing from US President Donald Trump, with whom Leo, first American pontiff, has publicly disagreed, particularly on the treatment of migrants and the war in Iran. The pope’s visit comes at a time when Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism and has also been accused of undermining democracy through attacks on the press and divisive rhetoric. He has also struggled to secure bipartisan agreements. “Democracy, then, is also a part of Argentina’s heritage that needs to be safeguarded,” the pope said at a meeting with politicians, members of civic society and the diplomatic corps at the Palacio Libertad. “Democracy is also strengthened by the daily conduct of public life: through willingness to listen, through careful use of words, through the patient search for agreement, and through the ability to see those who think differently as fellow citizens with whom we share a common future.” The Chicago-born pontiff, who recently cast a mail-in ballot during the US mid-term elections, talked about the importance of the “freedom to elect one’s own leaders through the ballot box.” He urged leaders to recognize the limits of their power, and said that democracy is protected by “confidence in the law”, the ability to freely express convictions and for institutions to serve all parties. “Authority is most authentic when it is exercised as service, when it looks beyond the immediate, and when it uses its power to promote the welfare of all,” the pope said. An eruption of applause from the audience forced him to repeat his next line: “Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them.” Leo’s November 8-11 trip is the first papal visit to Argentina in almost four decades and it comes with the added dimension that Pope Francis did not make a return trip home during his 12-year-papacy. Millions are expected to attend the various services and events while the pope is in the country. Francis’ decision not to visit Argentina was something even his closest friends were unable to explain. Some have suggested the late pope’s reluctance to visit was linked to Argentina’s polarized political culture, with Francis wary that his presence in the country could be weaponized. The Argentine pope had a strong emphasis on the church helping the most marginalized in society. Francis lamented Argentina’s economic decline which he blamed on decades of bad governance. He contrasted the roughly 5% inflation rate he recalled from his youth with the soaring inflation and high poverty rates of recent years. In his speech, Leo cited Argentina’s “abundance of human resources” but called for its “wealth bear fruit for the benefit of all and warned that corruption undermines trust in institutions. Before his election as pope in 2013, Francis served as archbishop of Buenos Aires, where he spoke out on social justice and was unafraid to criticize political leaders. Leo’s visit, the second leg of his 12-day tour of South America, will underline the ways he continues the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style. Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary in Argentina includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts. During his presidential campaign and in the years leading up to it, Milei repeatedly insulted Francis, calling him an “imbecile” for defending social justice, “the representative of the evil one on earth” and a “sh*t of a pope.” Milei later apologized for these remarks and called Francis “the most important Argentine in history” following the pontiff’s death in April 2025, repeating the compliment in his remarks on Sunday. Milei and Francis met in the Vatican in February 2024, with the pope joking with the president: “you cut your hair!” — a reference to the unruly hairstyle which earned Milei the nickname “The Wig.” Milei replied that he had “tidied it up.” Leo and Milei previously met at the Vatican in June 2025. After meeting Milei in the Casa Rosada on his arrival in Buenos Aires, the pope was presented with the keys to the city of the Argentine capital by the mayor, Jorge Macri.

cnn.com.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair as company launches investigation into foreign spy claims
cnn.com.text: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital affair as his company announced it will investigate reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The separate statements come amid growing concern over Huang’s close relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, Alice Huang. Several US outlets have reported that American officials suspect Alice Huang, no relation, has fed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips into the country. The controversy could undermine faith in the world’s second-largest company and a poster child for the AI boom, at a time when the US and China are racing to surpass the other in technological supremacy. In a note to Nvidia staff, Huang said that he was “unfaithful” and hurt his wife and children. He did not name the other person in the affair. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang, 63, said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.” Meanwhile, the company said in a Sunday press release that a committee of independent directors and outside counsel will oversee its investigation. “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the statement said. But, the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” In a note, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at merchant bank Yorkville & Ives Co., called the news “a black eye moment for Jensen” that will increase scrutiny of chip sales to China, which Huang has previously lobbied for. The investigation will also cast a shadow over Nvidia’s share price, Ives added, as investors question whether Huang will remain at the helm of the company he helped found. “Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption,” a spokesperson for Nvidia told CNN. Jacob Ward, a tech journalist and CNN contributor said corporate boards historically tend to oust chief executives caught having extramarital affairs within days. For Nvidia, which holds an outsized role in AI development, global growth and the US stock market, any existential questions about its future will have even greater economic and geopolitical implications. Another unusual factor is that the company has no clear successor for Huang, he added. “It is a core of the American economy, if not the world economy right now. And this guy who is famously a very, very central commander of all of this stuff, suddenly being caught in this way and especially being caught perhaps being dishonest about it, it’s an incredibly big deal,” Ward said. The China connection Huang’s connections to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, which buys chips from Nvidia, have come under intense scrutiny as a potential channel for US semiconductors to reach Chinese buyers, despite export controls on advanced technologies. The Financial Times previously reported that US intelligence believed that the two were in a romantic relationship. Nvidia said in a past statement that Jensen Huang’s meetings were “not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” It added that any concerns about illegal chip diversion were “debunked last year.” Huang joked in a previous interview that he wooed his wife Lori Huang, whom he met in college when he was 17 and she was 19, by offering to help with her homework and vowing to become a CEO by age 30. The couple married in 1985 and have two children. In 1993 he co-founded Nvidia, which has seen its market capitalization swell to more than $4 trillion as the rise of AI has turbocharged demand for the computer chips it designs. He has since become the face of the company and a prominent figure in the booming business of AI. Huang joined President Donald Trump with a host of other high-profile CEOs in Beijing earlier this year to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. “Nvidia and Jensen are deeply intertwined. Many people will say Nvidia without Jensen won’t be the same,” George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, wrote in a Monday note. “I don’t think it will serve the best interests of Nvidia shareholders and industry partners either if Jensen suddenly quits tomorrow.” The US government cleared 10 Chinese firms to buy Nvidia’s second-most powerful AI chips, Reuters reported earlier this year, though its unclear how many chips have actually been sold following the approval. On Sunday, Trump told reporters that he has not spoken to Huang since Nvidia announced the investigation, but said that he was a “fine person” and praised his contribution to the country. When asked if he wished he had taken action when briefed on the intelligence about alleged spying last year, Trump said, “No I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.” On Thursday, Republican chairmen of three influential House panels — the committees on Foreign Affairs, the Chinese Communist Party and Intelligence — said in a news release that they sent a letter to Huang requesting his appearance before their committees to answer questions about his relationship with Megaspeed and the company’s security protocols against foreign espionage. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that the allegation that Alice Huang was gathering information for Beijing was “purely groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.” State-run tabloid The Global Times accused US media outlets of making up stories that could derail a detente between the two nations. On Chinese social media, Huang’s admission of infidelity became one of the top trending topics with more than 40 million views on the X-like platform Weibo. However, the allegation that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese spy was largely absent from tightly-controlled online discussions. This story has been updated with additional content.

cnn.com.title: Trump says renewed attacks on Iran ‘highly unlikely’ if talks show progress
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump said on Sunday that it is “highly unlikely” he will need to order the US back to war with Iran as long as there is progress in negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, repeating his assertion five times during an interview with CNN. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN’s Jim Sciutto during a 20-minute phone interview, referring to Iran. “The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.” “So it’s highly unlikely I’ll have to,” he continued. “They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off.” ‘We’re ready for it’ Eight months after the war started, the two sides have been in a stalemate, with little military action or significant diplomatic progress made while oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz have come under Iranian attack. The two countries and officials from Qatar, which has mediated the talks, have kept quiet about the status of their negotiations. But Iranian hardliners have seized on the results of last week’s midterm elections — fueled in part by the war’s unpopularity with US voters — as a sign of a weakened Trump presidency that would be more willing to given in to their country’s demands to be allowed to continue its nuclear program, which it says it needs for energy, and maintain control of the strait. Iran has also struggled to sell crude oil on global markets under US sanctions, while billions of dollars in assets held in foreign banks have been frozen. Meanwhile, the US military has begun offering a reward of up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear program and has launched a task force aimed at blocking Tehran from using land routes to move advanced weapons and other materials — signs that Washington is intensifying pressure rather than easing it. Trump, who has in the past offered mixed messages about his willingness to end the war, made clear during the interview that US forces are in position in the region if he were to give the order to strike. “We’re ready for it. I’ve got three aircraft carriers here. The other one just arrived. We have three. They’re fully locked and loaded,” he said. The president also said that the US has identified infrastructure targets inside Iran in the event of renewed military action, including power plants and bridges. “We have 38 bridges in our site that we can knock down in literally one hour, “ he said. “They’ll all be down.” However, he said he would prefer not to destroy Iranian infrastructure. “I don’t want to do that because essentially, it’ll take 10 years to rebuild them,” he said. “I don’t like ripping down bridges. And the hardest thing to build is a bridge. It takes years, and I’m a good builder.” Diplomatic activity across the Middle East has increased since Tuesday’s midterm elections. On Friday, Qatar said that Trump had called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss de-escalation, and a day earlier, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke with his counterparts from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Pakistan, Kuwait, Jordan, Turkey, Cyprus and Qatar. Before leaving on Sunday for the G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a resolution in the talks did not appear to be close. “I wouldn’t say we’re on the verge of a breakthrough,” he told reporters in Florida. “Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.” Depleted Iranian stockpiles In terms of Iran’s ability to defend against new US strikes, Trump said Iran’s air defenses have been destroyed. “It’s unstoppable because they have no anti-aircraft stuff. All of their anti-aircraft is gone,” he said. The president also provided new details on the state of Iranian missile and drone stockpiles, saying that the regime maintains 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capabilities. “The only thing they can do is about 10% level — make some missiles and make some drones. Drones at about 15% because much of their factories are gone,” he said. “Most likely it will not be necessary,” he repeated about the prospect of new military action. “They want to make a deal so badly.”

cnn.com.title: MAHA makes its case to Democrats as blue wave crashes GOP alliance and threatens RFK Jr.
cnn.com.text: One day after the blue wave that swept away dozens of Republican seats, the mood among Make America Healthy Again activists was palpably glum. On a weekly Wednesday call hosted by MAHA Action, the most prominent political fundraising group for the movement, the normally enthusiastic atmosphere was replaced by pep talks from its founder Tony Lyons and advocates active in its circles. Zach Lahn, the losing Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate who had been MAHA’s first endorsement of the midterms, sought to downplay the scale of the rout, putting it down to “a terrible cycle”. In the wake of the stunning Republican defeat, some are openly asking whether to recast their message to appeal to Democrats on bipartisan issues. “The partial fracture we’ve seen between MAHA and MAGA in some ways may be a good thing. It’s important that MAHA not be a partisan issue,” Joseph Ladapo, Florida’s surgeon general and a vaccine skeptic, said on the call. But while some Democrats have expressed an openness to courting MAHA allies whose concerns about healthy food and the environment can be common ground, a pivot would present an enormous test to a movement that for the past two years married its cause to President Donald Trump’s ‘Make America Great Again’ base and his divisive Health and Human Services Secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Democratic leadership and incoming senators are promising investigations and even a possible impeachment vote for Kennedy, who they see as the face of disease outbreaks and federal upheaval over health care. “We ought to be pursuing some corrections to the chaos, the cost, and the corruption that’s running rapid in Washington today, and we can do that by moving to make these people account for their actions,” Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina told CNN’s Pamela Brown on Friday, naming Kennedy and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the House majority’s top two targets. Incoming Democratic senators, including South Carolina’s Annie Andrews and Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed — both doctors — have echoed that sentiment, putting them at early odds with MAHA voters who see opportunities to work with Democrats on popular issues like access to healthier food. Even Trump has warned that shifts should be expected, telling CBS’s 60 Minutes: “”I love my Cabinet. I think they’re good. But I’ll … be doing maybe a few changes.” Whether Trump has Kennedy in mind or not, some Democrats have made it clear he’s in their crosshairs. “Unless RFK Jr. is interested in spending the next two years in front of Congressional committees, he should go ahead and resign now,” Sen. Ralph Warnock of Georgia posted to X. An HHS spokesperson said in a statement: “Secretary Kennedy has delivered the most sweeping public health reforms in modern history.” “Threats of impeachment will not distract him from delivering for the American people.” A tough pivot – but an opportunity? Three tent poles make up the MAHA movement — a drive for healthier food, demand for environmental safety and advocacy for ‘medical freedom,’ or vaccine choice. There have always been both fractures and overlaps within the movement, said David Mansdoerfer, a former deputy assistant secretary for health during the first Trump administration. But in the new political environment, these interests will more clearly diverge, he said. “MAHA as an electoral body is an important one for both parties, but MAHA isn’t a like, single policy issue,” said Mansdoerfer, a proponent of medical freedom, which he said is “pretty staunchly built into the Republican platform” and unlikely to find Democratic allies. Democrats swept Republican MAHA allies from office, including Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, who most notably backed the medical freedom vein of its platform and snubbed new contenders like Lahn. But at the same time, even incoming senators who have tussled with Kennedy spot opportunities to court MAHA voters. El-Sayed in September debuted an agenda for a ‘Healthier America’ that promises to tackle toxins in food, agriculture and water — core tenets of the grassroots movement. El-Sayed and some other Democrats are less likely to court the “anti-vaxxers” but see important strides to be made with “organic and pesticide moms,” said Celinda Lake, a Democratic pollster who worked with El-Sayed’s campaign. “That is very important because it’s a big suburban audience and there is a real possibility of making gains.” Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democratic Maine congresswoman who has long pitched making inroads with MAHA voters, launched the Fix Our Food Caucus this fall. She said she did so “to try to give a little a little bit of perspective on the things that we think are most important to the broadest group of people.” “I’m willing to work with anyone on the White House in this administration, when we can make some gains on things we care about, but not to support any of their negative agenda,” Pingree told CNN on Friday. “If RFK survives all this, I hope we can get the focus back on healthier foods, food is medicine, and straighten out the CDC and vaccine side of it.” Asked in a text message if there are Democrats he is hopeful about working with, Lyons, the MAHA Action founder, replied: “I’m always hopeful!!!” The Kennedy question Pingree, who will assume chairmanship of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies, says she is looking for accountability. “I don’t think Democrats will have a huge impeachment agenda, but I think we have so much work — investigating, subpoenaing, getting down to records, looking for collusion,” she said. She told CNN that when Democrats take over in January she is “absolutely” going to call in Lee Zeldin, director of the Environmental Protection Agency,  over deregulation of environmental toxins and the administration’s work with Bayer, the main manufacturer of commonly used herbicide glyphosate — another major target for MAHA supporters. In the Senate, both El-Sayed and Annie Andrews, the South Carolina Democratic senator-elect and pediatrician — who has called Kennedy a “grifter” – have said they would launch impeachment proceedings against the health secretary. His harshest critics have accused him of spreading misinformation, dismantling government grant distributions and undermining public health, arguing these are grounds for impeachment. But it’s a delicate balance for Democrats. The common thread holding MAHA voters together is Kennedy. “All three of those factions are still very supportive of Secretary Kennedy, and a lot of them will look at how he is treated in this process to whether they can fully feel like they can work in a bipartisan manner,” Mansdoerfer said. Prominent MAHA advocates such as Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America, have publicly warned that impeaching Kennedy would be a “colossal mistake” for Democrats. “Any of those independents who consider Kennedy their champion — which I would say is probably most of them — are not going to vote Democrat at all ever if they mess with Kennedy,” she argued on the MAHA Action call. In the meantime, the Trump administration appears to be digging its heels in on some of its core priorities. On Saturday, the president called on the Justice department to investigate Democrats he said were “going around threatening” impeachment. In a sign of the ongoing fallout from the midterms rout, Trump on Friday announced that his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, was leaving and being replaced with Stephen Miller. The announcement came within an hour of longtime MAHA advocate and former White House advisor Calley Means sharing on social media a two-hour podcast that laid most of the blame for stalled progress on Wiles and corporate interests in DC. “Susie Wiles is the most powerful chief of staff in modern American history, and she has taken a stranglehold on any policy decision,” Means, a close Kennedy ally, said on the Joe Rogan Experience. “Every single cabinet secretary, they’re spending meetings constantly worrying about how to get on Susie’s good side.” Kennedy swiftly praised Miller’s appointment to chief of staff, citing his bonafides as a MAHA supporter. “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken,” the health secretary wrote Friday on X. His allies, meanwhile, issued a challenge to Democrats. “Let’s go Bobby,” Means posted on X Friday afternoon. “Democrats said they wanted to fix these things too, We can achieve histor[ic] reform in the next year.” Adam Cancryn contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Two trains collide in Egypt, killing 7 people and injuring more than 100, authorities say
cnn.com.text: At least seven people were killed and 112 people injured after two trains collided in Egypt on Sunday, the country’s health ministry said. Several carriages were derailed after one train collided with the rear of another between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Giza, near the capital Cairo, the Egyptian National Railways Authority said in a statement. Dozens of ambulances were dispatched to transport the injured to nearby hospitals, while cranes were deployed to remove the wreckage after traffic on the railroad was disrupted, Egyptian authorities said. Among the dozens injured in the collision, 45 people have been discharged from nearby hospitals after their condition improved, according to the health ministry. The Egyptian railway system, the oldest in Africa and the Middle East, has a long history of deadly accidents. In 2019, a train lost control while approaching Cairo’s main station in Ramses Square, igniting a fire that killed 25 people. Another accident in 2017 occurred on the way to Alexandria, when a train derailed and collided head-on with another train, killing more than 40 people. Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered an investigation into the Giza collision on Sunday, according to statement on his official Facebook page. He also offered his “sincere condolences” to those killed. This story has been updated.

cnn.com.title: Hiding in plain sight? Russell Brand’s conviction poses tough questions for UK entertainment industry
cnn.com.text: The judge presiding over Russell Brand’s criminal court case says the comedian will be handed down a lengthy prison sentence Monday after he was found guilty in a London court of raping a young fan and sexually assaulting three women. While that much is certain, other questions remain, including one that is worryingly familiar in the UK, a country that has seen the downfall of a host of celebrities accused of sexual offenses. How did he evade justice for so long? The 51-year-old former stand-up comedian’s conviction and the flurry of reaction from those who once moved in his orbit comes at a time of heightened debate in Britain about the toxic mix of fame, power and abuse. Britain’s Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said Sunday that sexual abuse remained a problem in the media industry. “Hand on heart I can’t say ‌to you as the ⁠culture secretary that this is not happening today and in fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is,” she told the BBC. She warned that women were often too afraid to report offenses as “speaking up has ​a very ‌heavy ​cost.” Just this week, the popular TV show Married at First Sight UK was axed following an investigation into rape allegations, according to Channel 4, at the same time as British media reported that an unnamed celebrity is attempting to block the publication of his name in relation to sexual misconduct allegations. After Brand’s guilty verdict, London’s Metropolitan Police superintendent said in a statement that as his profile grew during his acting and comedy career, “so too did his sense of entitlement.” The Met police also confirmed investigations are continuing regarding two further allegations of rape made against Brand. Prosecutors are assessing whether to bring additional charges, according to Britain’s Press Association (PA). “I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be,” senior police officer Andy Furphy said. But that statement has done little to hold back a wave of concern about the seeming immunity of some powerful figures to skirt accountability.
