A mix of grief and relief Responding to the verdict, British actress Sarah Solemani, who starred in the Bafta-winning sitcom “Him & Her,” said in an op-ed that Brand is finally facing justice but warned that other abusers are “still hiding in plain sight.” She said the comedy industry has “for some strange reason, brought me into the close orbit of more than your average number of sexual predators, several of whom are still merrily working.” “I had to pull a project from a company when I was informed it was common knowledge that a high-level exec was known for allegedly raping a colleague. Another famous comic had to pull a project when I informed them a legend they were working with was also an alleged rapist,” she wrote in the Guardian on Friday. Comedian Katherine Ryan, who worked with Brand on a comedy show in 2018, also responded to the verdict, saying on her podcast that she felt “grief” and “relief,” while commending the bravery of the survivors who “came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money (and) a legion of fans ready to attack them.” As well as figures within the comedy circuit, British broadcasters have also found themselves in the crossfire. After Brand’s conviction, the BBC reissued a statement about the celebrity’s controversial stint at the broadcaster in the 2000s, saying it was of “great concern to us that some people felt unable to raise concerns about Brand’s behaviour.” “We apologised to those impacted, for both the culture and failings at the time, and we reiterate that apology again today,” the BBC said. Brand’s convictions date back to 2004, 2005 and 2009, the decade when Brand moved from alternative comedy on a radically twisting path that took him to British television, Hollywood and eventually the world of podcasting and conspiracy theories. In 2006, Brand began co-hosting “The Russell Brand Show” on BBC Radio 2, a weekly Saturday night program during which he had frank, comedic and often X-rated conversations with a co-host and guests. However, the popular radio show ended abruptly two years later with Brand’s exit after the comedian and his co-host left a series of misogynistic voice messages for famed actor and “Fawlty Towers” star Andrew Sachs about his granddaughter. During a live radio segment, Brand and his then-co-presenter Jonathan Ross made lewd remarks about Brand’s relationship with Sachs’ granddaughter, Georgina Baillie, with the incident prompting several resignations and sparking a national backlash. Baillie sent her support to Brand’s victims following Thursday’s verdict while speaking about the devastating impact the BBC scandal had on her life. “Justice has been served. Although he never raped or assaulted me as I have always said, I didn’t know what happened in the privacy of the rooms that the victims and Russell were in and their evidence was compelling,” she told Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. “I now want Russell to right the wrongs.” Brand’s exposure represents the latest in a string of historic abuse investigations into former BBC stars, including sex offenders Rolf Harris and Jimmy Savile who were both staples of family television during their heyday. “There can be no place for the abuse of power. Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else’s hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to,” a BBC spokesperson said in a statement. ‘A matter of regret for our industry’ Allegations of rape and sexual assault against Brand were made public in a joint 2023 investigation by three British media outlets – The Sunday Times, The Times and Channel 4’s “Dispatches” program. Brand has denied the allegations in the program, which related to multiple women who were not involved in the criminal trial. Esella Hawkey, the executive producer of the documentary, “Russell Brand: In Plain Sight,” said she was pleased with the verdict but added that she “would much rather these events not have happened in the first place.” Speaking about how Brand evaded justice for so long, Hawkey told CNN it can be “very difficult” for individuals to challenge “so-called talent and very big names who, you know, have a huge monetary value for the broadcasters.” “I think television and broadcasting does have a problem with dealing with that behavior and also in enabling people,” she said. “I really do hope that this is an opportunity for the industry to do some inward looking.” On Thursday, the director of news at Channel 4, Louise Compton, said “the trial heard that women involved in the criminal case came forward after seeing the Channel 4 Dispatches film,” while commending the courage of the women involved. The TV channel’s role in spotlighting the former comedian’s behaviour has not made it immune from criticism. Following the 2023 revelations, Channel 4 announced it had opened an investigation into whether people at the channel were aware of Brand’s behavior while he was engaged in programs made for the broadcaster between 2004 and 2007. The network said the investigation did not find any evidence to suggest Channel 4 employees were aware of Brand’s behavior documented in the expose, but then-CEO of Channel 4 Alex Mahon apologized over a separate allegation about Brand in 2009 that she said was not investigated as it should have been. “In my view, it is a matter of regret for our industry that repugnant behaviours were tolerated – and indeed appeared on-air – in the past,” Mahon said. National Sexual Assault Hotline 1-800-656-4673; Provided by RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network). Available 24/7. Also available through online chat tool.

cnn.com.title: The vanity economy is taking over America’s downtowns
cnn.com.text: QQ Nails opened its first salon in New York City twenty years ago. By 2020, QQ had grown to roughly 20 locations. It’s nearly doubled in size since the pandemic. Thirty-eight QQ salons now dot the city’s streets, with plans for dozens more. In one six block radius in Manhattan, there are four. “People are more willing to spend on self-care, self-expressiveness and these types of larger services,” CEO Tian Jiang said. Welcome to the “vanity economy.” Brick-and-mortar stores were once designed to sell you stuff: shoes, furniture and TVs. Today, they’re all about making your face, abs, hair and nails look and feel fit for the world— both the in-person and social media versions of your life. City streets and suburban shopping malls have been reconfigured in response to our collective obsession with appearance, health and performance. The transformation of retail storefronts is the physical manifestation of marketing buzzwords like “looksmaxxing,” “self-care” and “longevity.” Nail salons on every block. Med spas expanding rapidly. Pilates chains opening hundreds of clubs. High-intensity weightlifting studios, bathhouses, saunas, stretching studios, cryotherapy and IV therapy. Nationwide, more than 1 out of every 4 retail leases signed in the United States this year has been from a cosmetics, beauty service or fitness company, according to CoStar. It’s on pace to be the highest annual share on record. Physical stores to help you look good online The presence of screens everywhere helps explain the changes in the physical commercial landscape. People want to look good when they see others in real life. They also want to look good on Instagram, Hinge and TikTok. Vanity businesses serve both our in-person and digital lives simultaneously. “There is definitely ‘aesthetic creep’ that has intensified in recent years” Natalia Mehlman Petrzela, a historian of American politics and culture at The New School, said in an email. Women and gay men have long felt pressure to present themselves, but “straight men are now encompassed by the beauty-industrial complex in new ways” than the pre-looksmaxxing, social media era. Physical retail has also changed because many younger consumers prioritize smaller acts of self-improvement in an economy where traditional life milestones such as homeownership, marriage and kids, feel out of reach. Increasingly living alone and staying single, these consumers are less willing to cut back on gym memberships and manicures that help them feel healthier, stronger and more attractive. Gym and fitness studio memberships for people under 35 are growing faster than older groups, and they spend more on their monthly gym dues than older generations, according to the Health & Fitness Association. Gen Z spending at cosmetics stores was also nearly twice as strong as the overall average this year. When QQ Nails opened in 2006, manicures were seen as a “pampering moment,” Jiang said. “All you did was a polish and a clean up.” But manicures and personal care services are now associated with physical and mental well-being. Salons’ offerings and techniques have evolved, too. More expensive gel manicures and pedicures replaced regular air-dried nail polish. Customers come for extensions and custom designs they see on TikTok. More men get manicures. “It’s become more ingrained in everybody’s routines,” she said. Amazon-proof Vanity businesses have also come to dominate the streets because e-commerce has altered the utility of a storefront. As online shopping made it easier than ever to buy products from home, physical retail moved into services that couldn’t easily be duplicated online. Amazon can ship a television or pair of sneakers to your doorstep. But it can’t give you a manicure, Botox or six-pack abs. Retail leasing by service-oriented tenants outpaced goods-based tenants for the first time ever this year. It’s a shift for real estate developers and city planners who were long wary of gyms and personal-care businesses in prime retail corridors. Cities have loosened their zoning laws to make it easier for gyms, studios and spas to expand into more commercial areas in recent years. Many traditional retailers in shopping centers ended strict provisions in their leases preventing fitness tenants from locating nearby. As these lease restrictions eased, shopping centers added more boutique fitness tenants, said David Gerstenhaber, the head of leasing at Brixmor Property Group. The company owns more than 340 shopping centers around the country. Forty percent of Brixmor’s shopping centers now have a boutique fitness tenant, up from 29% in 2021. Beauty, boutique fitness, and wellness tenants like Face Foundrie and Hydration Room have grown 11% over the last five years at its properties. Lake Pointe Village, a shopping center in Sugar Land, Texas, anchored by Whole Foods, is the poster child for the shift. There are 13 vanity businesses in the center — everything from Solidcore to VIO Med Spa to European Wax Center. “It all comes down to look good, feel good,” he said.

cnn.com.title: CNN analysis uncovers construction flaws in public housing towers that collapsed during Venezuela quakes
cnn.com.text: The day after massive dual earthquakes shattered Venezuela, Ailin Quiroz made her way toward the coast to search for her sister. She found only a mountain of rubble where her apartment building had once stood. Quiroz climbed through the ruins for hours but found no trace of her sister or six other relatives who lived in the 13-story tower. Now, she’s tormented by a question: Why did their building collapse while other nearby high-rises survived? The building was one of 15 public housing towers in the coastal town of Caraballeda that collapsed in the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes on June 24. Though the government has yet to release a comprehensive list of people killed, thousands of public housing residents likely perished in the disaster. Each tower, over eight stories tall, had at least 240 apartments. A CNN analysis of videos and images of some of those buildings — both during an extraordinarily fast construction process and after their collapse — suggests that construction flaws may have contributed to the mass tragedy. That visual evidence appears to show improperly assembled rebar supports — steel bars meant to reinforce the strength of concrete — in apparent building code violations at five government-built complexes, where the 15 collapsed towers once stood. In three of the complexes, images also show deep-seated rust in metal supports, which experts say could be a sign of poor-quality concrete. It is unclear whether these building defects were present in every government-built tower that fell. Experts in structural engineering, Venezuelan building practices, and seismology who reviewed evidence of the defects said those faults could have made the towers more prone to collapsing in massive earthquakes, though they also cautioned that it’s difficult to prove a direct cause following the massive tremors. “This is how a concrete structure fails if it’s not done right,” structural engineer Kit Miyamoto explained while on the ground in Caracas. Immediately after the earthquakes, a government commission was established to analyze affected buildings. Nearly 100 buildings are being analyzed using material samples and measurements, commission President Francisco Garcés told CNN. One disaster to the next For nearly a decade, residents had complained of problems in the towers, which were commissioned in 2011 by then-Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez. Local media reported dozens of residents’ complaints about persistent water intrusion, damaged pipes, and sewage leaks. The 15 towers that later fell were among dozens built across Venezuela by the Chávez regime, many intended to house families displaced by a flooding and landslide disaster in 2010. Located near the San Sebastián fault line on Venezuela’s coast, their construction came under the responsibility of the Presidential Office of Special Plans and Projects (OPPPE), which Chávez had created two years earlier as part of his sweeping ambition to build three million homes in nine years. These housing developments were constructed in barely a year. The Office of Special Plans and Projects’ then director and chief architect — Chávez’s longtime friend Francisco Sesto — detailed the process in his personal blog, writing that the president demanded 200,000 homes to be built in 2012 alone, the year of their construction. Former OPPPE principal Lucas Pou told CNN it was standard practice for the Office to award no-bid contracts under an emergency directive to help speed things along but said he hadn’t worked on the Caraballeda housing projects. In his blog, Sesto describes the OPPPE’s mission as “a gigantic effort carried out with an intensity never before seen in Venezuela.” To stay on schedule, he wrote, construction teams rotated through two to three shifts every day. Sesto did not respond to CNN’s multiple requests for comment on this story but told The New York Times that he does not consider it “journalistically sound to focus on a handful of Great Mission buildings that collapsed, given that hundreds of private buildings also collapsed.” While tens of thousands of buildings were likely damaged or destroyed in the quakes, these OPPPE developments were among the largest residential buildings to fall in coastal La Guaira state. Satellite imagery shows that in Caraballeda, 63% of all high-rise towers built by a special public housing authority collapsed. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez ordered the suspension of the OPPPE in February, a few months before the earthquakes. Rebar issues Venezuela’s 2006 building code — which was in effect when the buildings were constructed — required that short pieces of rebar, or “stirrups,” be bent to 135-degree angles in every high-rise building across La Guaira. This safeguard makes it harder for earthquakes to break or unseat the ties that reinforce beams and columns. But images captured across these five complexes (each comprised of several individually built towers) during their construction starting in 2011 and after the 2026 earthquakes show that some stirrups appeared to be bent to only 90 degrees. This difference likely violated Venezuelan building regulations, and experts say it could be the difference between a structure failing catastrophically or holding together during a severe earthquake. During strong seismic shaking, just a few improperly assembled stirrups could compromise the integrity of a beam or column, said Jeffrey Dowgala and Terrence Paret, structural engineers with expertise in earthquake resilience at Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates. Miyamoto, a structural engineer who has led post-earthquake damage assessments around the world, most recently in Venezuela, likened the stirrups defect to a wine barrel without properly assembled steel straps. Following the quakes, Miyamoto and his team of roughly 100 engineers have worked under Venezuela’s Ministry of Public Works to assess the structural integrity of surviving buildings. Venezuela’s Communications Ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Miyamoto told CNN the stirrup fabrication issue was pervasive in the rubble of buildings he assessed in La Guaira. He also stressed that these rebar implementation failures were present in public and private buildings alike. A photograph taken during an OPPPE inspection of one construction site in March 2012 appears to show several stirrups containing the defect at the foundation of one tower in the complex known as OPPPE 27. All four towers at that site collapsed when the earthquakes hit 14 years later. Multiple photos of the same complex’s ruins following the earthquakes show that at least some of those defective stirrups were never rectified, experts said. Of more than 40 photos and videos CNN verified that specifically showed the stirrups, only a small minority were clearly bent properly. Images of at least two fallen complexes highlight another possible issue with the buildings’ rebar supports: they appear to be spaced closely but are only rarely bundled, as the 2006 code requires. To comply with the code, rebar strands must either be bundled together to act as a single unit or be separated by a gap of at least one bar diameter — and sometimes more, depending on their placement. This, too, can degrade the structural integrity of a concrete building, experts say, and underscores inconsistencies in the building techniques used. The condition of the rebar, exposed after the buildings collapsed, has also raised concerns. Footage captured after the quakes appears to show deep-seated rust in rebar in at least three collapsed OPPPE complexes; about half of collapsed buildings in this area bore signs of corrosion, Miyamoto estimates. Caraballeda’s tropical, beachfront climate could have been a factor, as well as possible impurities in the concrete used, which can eat away at the metal bars. Two construction workers who worked on one of the public housing complexes told The New York Times their team stretched materials by mixing other products into the concrete. The Times also found that the towers had no visible shear walls, and that the uniform orientation of their columns weakened these high-rises against seismic forces. Resident accounts also described issues symptomatic of poor-quality concrete. One neighbor, who often visited friends in OPPPE 26, recounted how “the floor would crack from any impact.” For her part, Quiroz doesn’t recall any similar incidents, nor did she witness any major water or sewage leaks. In October of 2025, a resident of OPPPE 26 told La Verdad that his wife was injured when a chunk of their living room ceiling dislodged and fell on her. “Luckily, she was able to cover her head and only suffered a shoulder injury,” he recalled in an interview with La Verdad de Vargas. An open question Today, several towers built by the special office remain standing — some not far from the Caraballeda complex where Quiroz’s sister died. Just over half a mile east from the Caraballeda towers stands another complex built by the special office and comprised of nearly 700 apartments. Of its seven towers, five survived this year’s twin earthquakes. They have now been evacuated and displaced residents are camping in tents outside, according to María Sánchez, a resident who spoke to CNN. It is unclear whether those buildings will be put back into use. A 2012 photo taken during construction of the complex, named OPPPE 25, shows rebar stirrups assembled with the same 90-degree bends. CNN reached out to the Venezuelan government and the office of the mayor of La Guaira, José Manuel Suárez Maldonado, but is yet to hear back. CNN’s Thomas Bordeaux and Abel Alvarado contributed to this report. Clarification: This story has been updated to reflect the latest estimated figures of buildings likely damaged or destroyed in the quakes.

cnn.com.title: How the rejection of Trump produced a biblical downpour on Republicans
cnn.com.text: From the weakest to the strongest Republican candidates, from purple to ruby-red terrain, hardly anyone in the GOP escaped untouched by last week’s ferocious roar from American voters. It was a night when, to paraphrase the Bible, the electoral rain fell on the just and the unjust alike. Tactical campaign decisions and financial advantages, or even candidate quality cannot explain movement of this magnitude and consistency; change this big flows only from a current broad and deep enough to cut through the entire country. That current wasn’t hard to identify: towering discontent with President Donald Trump’s tumultuous second term. In the Voter Poll conducted by SSRS for CNN and a consortium of other news organizations, as of the Friday after the elections, just 37% of voters approved of Trump’s performance as president, while 63% disapproved. That was a significantly greater level of disapproval than Trump faced in 2018 — or that Barack Obama in 2010, George W. Bush in 2006 and Bill Clinton in 1994 confronted in midterm elections that also routed their parties. As the veteran Democratic pollster Celinda Lake told me in October, across her more than four decades in politics, Trump is now facing “the broadest sense we’ve had that a president has failed. It is broader than it was in 2018 for him, or even for George W. Bush in 2006.” That wave of discontent surged over the walls that Republican had hoped would contain it — their advantages in money and the map of states and districts being contested. Democrats made dramatic breakthroughs in House, Senate, governor and state legislative races in every region. Voter polls showed them recording significant gains among the big voter groups that moved toward Trump in 2024 — including Latinos and young adults — while also improving among the electorate’s key swing groups (such as independents and college-educated White men) and benefiting from robust turnout among their traditional core supporters. Democrats seized multiple Senate seats in states that had only elected Republicans for decades. Unusually strong Democratic candidates (such as Senate victors Adam Hamilton in Kansas and James Talarico in Texas, or House winners Cait Conley in New York and Bobby Pulido in Texas) and unusually weak Republican candidates (including losing Senate nominees Roger Marshall in Kansas, Darline Graham in South Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas) help explain some of those seismic shifts. But Democrats won plenty of races with only average candidates, and undeniably talented Republicans like New York’s Mike Lawler, Pennsylvania’s Brian Fitzpatrick and Iowa’s Ashley Hinson were swept away with the laggards, too. The problem for those Republicans was that the name on the back of the jersey didn’t matter as much to furious voters as the red color of the front. The impact of that consensus was immediately evident in every race and every county that we flagged as markers for how the election might go. The early signals The headwinds facing Republicans were clear in two of the East Coast states we thought would provide the best early gauge of how high the wave would grow. In the VA-2 House race, Democrat Elaine Luria comfortably ousted Republican Jen Kiggans in a contest that showed the party on track for a solid night. Democrat Shannon Taylor narrowly edged Republican Rob Wittman in VA-1, a district Trump carried by 5 points in 2024. That was an early sign that the wave was reaching deeper into Republican territory. In Pennsylvania, Democrats comfortably flipped seats at each level of difficulty. Double-digit wins for Democrat Bob Brooks against Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in PA-7 and Janelle Stelson over Republican Rep. Scott Perry in PA-10 showed dramatic movement in two seats Trump won by 5 points or less. Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti’s nearly 9-point victory over Republican Rob Bresnahan in PA-8, a blue-collar northeastern Pennsylvania district Trump carried by 9 points, was an early sign of deeper distress for the GOP. Most striking was Democrat Bob Harvie’s comfortable 5-point victory over Brian Fitzpatrick, who had defied all previous efforts to dislodge him from PA-1, a suburban Philadelphia district that usually voted blue for president. That was an early marker that even Republicans who had tried to build a reputation somewhat independent of Trump could not survive the powerful undertow of discontent with his second term. The same message was evident in Democrat Rebecca Bennett’s resounding double-digit win over Republican Tom Kean Jr. in NJ-7 and Conley’s solid 4-point victory over Lawler, a skilled and tenacious opponent, in the NY-17 seat stretching from affluent Westchester County into the Hudson Valley. But the force of the Trump undertow that would define the night first became fully apparent in the fall of Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. In 2020, during Trump’s first term, Collins was the only GOP Senate incumbent or challenger who won in a state where the exit polls showed more voters disapproved than approved of Trump’s job performance. The Voter Poll showed Collins on Tuesday again succeeded in attracting more voters who disapproved of Trump than almost any other Republican. But compared with 2020, more Maine voters this time disapproved of Trump (63%), and considerably more of those disapprovers supported Democrat Troy Jackson (80%) than backed her opponent in 2020 (71%). That tide of discontent with Trump’s performance carried Jackson to a comfortable 6-point win, even though 56% of voters said they did not believe the rough-hewn candidate had the right temperament for the job. Collins was a tall tree in the political forest. Once it became clear that the current was strong enough to dislodge even her durable roots, it seemed clear that other Republicans with shallower attachments would be swept away as well. The pattern extends Moving west and south, Democrats won, almost always easily, the other races we identified as signaling a good night for the party, including ousting House Republicans in WI-3, IA-1 and IA-3, and winning the open seat Iowa governor race, as well as the governor and Senate contests in Ohio. Most striking: Democrats across the Midwest ousted four House Republicans in strongly pro-Trump districts that we believed would fall only in a true tsunami: Ann Wagner and Victoria Spartz in the white-collar seats MO-2 and IN-5, and Michael Turner and Mike Carey in the more blue-collar seats of OH-10 and OH-15. Hamilton’s success in becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932 also pushed the night firmly into tsunami territory. In the South, Democrats won all the races they needed to for a good night (such as the reelection victories by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, Democratic Rep. Don Davis in NC-1 and Democratic House incumbents who beat gerrymanders in FL-14 and FL-25), as well as tougher contests such as Keisha Lance Bottoms’ history-making triumph in the Georgia governor race. But, as in the Midwest, Southern Democrats also scored some truly historic wins. The headline so far was Annie Andrews’ Senate win in South Carolina (a state Trump won by nearly 18 points just two years ago). Democrats also notched tsunami-level wins in North Carolina House seats — including narrowly beating Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, in NC-9, a district Trump carried by almost 16 points. A win for Democrat Scott Colom in the Mississippi Senate race, which appears within reach as final ballots are tallied, would mark an even greater historic breakthrough for the party. Texas was where all these trends converged most powerfully. Democrats posted solid wins by defending incumbents Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez, in TX-28 and TX-34, two heavily Hispanic South Texas districts that Republicans gerrymandered to weaken them. They won even tougher races in two other heavily Hispanic districts when sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia easily held the open seat of TX-35 and Pulido, a charismatic Tejano singer, routed Monica De La Cruz in TX-15-a district Trump had carried by almost 18 points. Democrats moved their gains into historic territory with Katy Stout’s victory in TX-23, a district that few considered within reach until recently. Any win for James Talarico against Paxton in the Texas Senate race would have marked a very good night for Democrats, who had not captured a Senate seat there since 1988. But Talarico’s 12-point,1.2 million-vote advantage pushed the result deep into historic territory. As impressive as Talarico’s victory was, even more remarkable was Gina Hinojosa’s win over three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott. While Talarico was well-funded, Hinojosa was overwhelmingly outspent. And while Paxton was a deeply flawed opponent, Abbott had been a dominant force in Texas politics for years. Yet Hinojosa crushed Abbott by about 700,000 votes to become the state’s first Latina governor — and record a victory that stands as the textbook definition of historic. The common themes Democrats posted a similar record across the West. They won all the races we identified as the minimum for a good night (including flipping Republican-held House seats in CA-22, CO-8 and AZ-1). They won several tougher races (including flipping MT-1, AZ-6, and CO-5). And they barreled into historic territory by capturing the NV-2 House district (which Trump carried by 14 points), with a plausible remaining chance to flip CO-4, another double-digit Trump district. The Alaska governor and Senate contests, both of which would represent significant breakthroughs for Democrats, probably won’t be settled until mid-November; Democrats are favored strongly in the former and narrowly in the latter. Our pre-election list of counties to watch fell out in a similar pattern. Democrats notched gains in each of the major groupings that we identified: urban centers, traditionally White suburbs, racially diverse suburbs, mostly working-class White counties we dubbed “blue-collar bellwethers,” Latino enclaves and rural redoubts. Measuring the swing in voting behavior compared with 2024 showed virtually every congressional district moving toward the Democrats. In states including North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Texas, virtually (or literally) every county moved toward the Democrats compared with 2024 in their Senate or governor races or both, according to the analysis of the Decision Desk HQ political website. The Voter Poll conducted by SSRS for CNN and a consortium of news organizations underscored how the disenchantment with Trump drove those shifts. Beyond Trump’s 63% disapproval rating, a stunning 62% said he prioritized his personal interests over the country’s; 64% said he had the wrong priorities; 66% said his policies had hurt, not helped, the economy. Strong majorities of voters expressing each of those views backed Democrats. The breadth of Trump’s decline hurt Republicans as much as the depth. During his first term, even as most voters nationally disapproved of his performance, Trump retained majority support in most Republican-leaning states — which helped the GOP oust several red-state Democratic senators in 2018. But this year, a majority of voters disapproved of Trump’s performance in every state where Democrats flipped a Republican-held Senate seat; his disapproval ranged from 55% in South Carolina, to 57% in Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, 59% in Texas, 62% in North Carolina and 63% in Maine. At least 85% of the voters who disapproved of Trump supported the Democratic Senate candidate in each of those states except Maine. That left those GOP candidates in too deep a hole to escape. (In the national House poll, 86% of voters who disapproved of Trump voted Democratic, a number similar to the levels for Obama, Bush and Clinton, though slightly below the mark for Trump in 2018.) And even in those previously Republican-leaning states, many of Trump’s specific initiatives faced majority opposition. Between 52% to 56% of voters in Florida, Georgia, Arizona and even Texas felt his immigration enforcement efforts had gone too far. (Two-thirds of Texas Hispanics felt that way.) Between 61% to 66% of voters in Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — the sort of blue-collar behemoths long considered most receptive to a protectionist trade agenda — said his tariffs had hurt the local economy. (Even majorities of non-college White voters in those states viewed the tariffs as harmful.) At least three-fifths of voters in Texas, South Carolina, Nevada and Georgia said Trump was wrong to attack Iran. All this discontent converged to produce last Tuesday’s historic repudiation of Trump and the GOP. When all races are called, Democrats could reach their biggest House majority since 2009 — or even since 1991. Democrats also could reach at least 55 Senate seats —something either party has done only three times since 2000. It’s too early to say these breakthroughs have provided Democrats a lasting edge in the 50-50 stalemate that has defined the competition between the two parties for almost the entire 21st century. Predictions of realignment from each side after even big wins in recent years have all been frustrated. But last week’s results represented an earthquake big enough to potentially reset the playing field. The Democratic wins will elevate to national leadership a diverse array of younger leaders that will bring new vitality into a party that many voters in recent years have seen as “doddering,” in the words of Democratic pollster Paul Maslin. And while the big Democratic wins in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and potentially even Mississippi would undoubtedly be harder to replicate with the larger and more blue-collar electorate of a presidential year, they at least open new pathways for the party to an Electoral College majority beyond the handful of swing states that have dominated recent presidential campaigns. If nothing else, the results shattered the hardening belief in both parties that Republicans had constructed impregnable fortifications across the 25 states that have voted for Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Those defenses haven’t crumbled, but they have cracked — and created the openings for new possibilities beyond the past quarter century’s unending trench warfare between two electoral coalitions that are utterly inimical in their vision for the country, but have been almost exactly equal in size.

cnn.com.title: How Democrats reshaped the Senate, in charts and maps
cnn.com.text: Two years after President Donald Trump carried much of the country’s political map, voters in some of his strongest states delivered a dramatic reversal Tuesday. Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats, including in states Trump won by double digits in 2024. The shifts were enormous: The Democratic margin improved by more than 25 percentage points in Texas and more than 20 points in Kansas and South Carolina. County-by-county election results show where those gains happened, from Democratic strongholds to places that remained solidly Republican. CNN closely examined county-level votes in seven states where Democrats flipped a Senate seat that had been held by a Republican — Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine and New Hampshire — and also Mississippi and Alaska, where the results were too still close to call on Thursday. Voters shifted toward Democrats in more than 780 of those states’ 800 counties — another illustration of the nearly uniform partisan movement by the electorate across the nation in House and Senate races. In some places, such as Texas, scores of counties remained heavily Republican but still saw movement away from the GOP. In Texas’ urban areas, which were already Democratic or trending in that direction, the shift was also visible and decisive. This chart shows how each state’s counties voted in the 2024 presidential election compared with the 2026 Senate contests. A key shift in Texas came in the Rio Grande Valley, a heavily Latino region that had been reliably Democratic for decades before swinging toward President Donald Trump in 2024 — and back toward Democrats this year. Cameron County, home to the city of Harlingen, saw a massive shift towards the Democratic challenger, James Talarico. He won the county by a 38.5 percentage-point margin en route to his Senate victory, the first for a Democrat since 1988. Similar shifts happened in Hidalgo and Webb counties, which are home to McAllen and Laredo, respectively. The shift that led to Talarico’s victory can be credited in part on a transforming “blue spine” of counties along Interstate 35. The swath of land through the middle of the state is home to Laredo, San Antonio, Austin, Waco and Dallas/Fort Worth. These 21 counties have been growing more Democratic, even as the party has been shutout of statewide offices for three decades. It first emerged to prominence in 2018, when Democratic former congressman Beto O’Rourke came close to defeating Republican Sen. Ted Cruz. Talarico carried the region by about 26 points, more than doubling O’Rourke’s 2018 high-water mark for a modern-era Senate campaign.

cnn.com.title: Hakeem Jeffries has a plan for Donald Trump and for his Democratic critics
cnn.com.text: Backstage in Virginia Beach the Saturday before the midterms, Hakeem Jeffries sat in a room by himself. He read over the speech he was about to give, versions of which he’d given dozens of times in all sorts of tough districts — first in his head, then mouthing the words and practicing how he’d throw his hands around for emphasis. Jeffries was there to campaign for Elaine Luria, the Navy veteran trying to win back the seat she lost in the 2022 midterms. He then rushed to Alabama to pump up Rep. Shomari Figures, whom Republicans targeted as part of an unprecedented mid-decade redistricting effort that Jeffries had spent more than a year fighting, state by state. At that point, Democrats needed to net three seats to win the House. Now, Jeffries is set to have a margin well into the dozens as the last races finish counting. Luria and Figures, each considered underdogs earlier in the year, both won. “A lot of people counted us out and claimed the Democratic Party was dead in the immediate aftermath of the 2024 election,” Jeffries told CNN a week later, speaking via Zoom from New York Democrats’ traditional post-election gathering in Puerto Rico. “And now it appears that we’ve roared to life.” Jeffries, 56, is set to become the first Black speaker in American history, leading a historically large majority in battle against a president who just picked his most hard-line aide as chief of staff. Until the Democratic presidential nominee emerges, Jeffries will be perhaps his party’s most important leader, defining the agenda that candidates will have to answer for as they fan out across early primary states. But he also takes the gavel with his party in perpetual existential churn, the many members who won in swing or Trump districts already worried about overreach that could empower Republicans — and an activist left wing labeling him a shill of corporate interests and big money. He’s heard the criticism and insults from liberals, seen the sombrero memes from conservatives, and knows that some people say he’s not Nancy Pelosi, who leaves Congress in January. He responds by comparing himself to his hometown basketball team, which just won its first NBA championship in 53 years. “My track record speaks for itself,” Jeffries told CNN in a pair of extensive interviews. “If I’m the Knicks right now — you can take all the incoming in the world that you want, but they can sit there and say, ‘Our track record speaks for itself,’ and mean it. Our view as House Democrats is that we have fought hard and battled Republicans on every single issue to get us to this point.” Jeffries smiles thinking back to February 2025, three months after Democrats’ devastating 2024 losses, when he stood at a press conference in the basement of the Capitol and said of the House GOP, “You’ve lectured America that you had a big mandate — where is it?” “It was always to me a combination of arrogance and incompetence that House Republicans in particular — who narrowly held on to their majority, notwithstanding Donald Trump’s overwhelming victory across the country in terms of the battleground states, would somehow convince themselves that they had an overwhelming mandate,” Jeffries said. During the interviews, Jeffries kept pointing to the scoreboard: all the wins in districts that Republicans tried to gerrymander Democrats out of, the incumbents he convinced to stick through uphill fights, the $826 million he raised — more than any other House leader, the places all over the country where he was seen as a benefit to appear for candidates like Luria, walking out to Mary J. Blige’s “Family Affair” and getting crowds riled up by talking about making him speaker. That final weekend, Jeffries wasn’t listing a number of seats he expected Democrats to win, but he knew enough from aides’ math that they were likely to get the majority — as he predicted a year and a half ago. “There were people who thought I was out of my mind when I made that statement and clearly meant it,” Jeffries told CNN. How he plans to deal with Trump Jeffries has been talking with Sen. Chuck Schumer, the current Democratic leader and a fellow Brooklynite, about how to try to corner Trump. The president in recent days has veered between saying he’d work with Democrats and threatening to become “Mr. Veto” while selling $40 “VETO” red hats. Jeffries told CNN he wants to use as a model this summer’s housing bill, which passed with bipartisan support and became law in July after the president let enough days go by without action. “Donald Trump decided not to sign it, but he also understood he couldn’t veto it,” Jeffries said. “Perhaps that’s a pathway forward as it relates to what’s going to happen into the future, which means the one thing you can guarantee is that Democrats are going to relentlessly work to get things done and then it will fall to Donald Trump to decide as to whether he’s willing to partner with us to make life more affordable for everyday Americans.” Asked whether Trump has called him since Tuesday, Jeffries skipped his standard long-winded answers for just, “No.” Asked whether he’d called Trump: “No.” He hasn’t spoken to the president or to Vice President JD Vance since their one Oval Office meeting in September 2025. Trump hasn’t said much publicly about Jeffries since he posted AI images of the Democrat wearing a cartoon sombrero in the aftermath of that meeting. Jeffries has never had a direct conversation with Stephen Miller, the incoming chief of staff, whose promotion he greeted by referring to Miller as a “malignant tumor.” In the spring, Jeffries took the unusual move of personally whipping votes on an Iran war powers resolution. He wanted every Democrat, even those cheering to see Ayatollah Ali Khamenei killed despite no congressional authorization, to vote for the resolution in opposition to the war. But that was less to appeal to voters on foreign policy or constitutional grounds, he thought, than to corner Republicans on gas prices. Ultimately, four Democrats broke with the rest of the caucus. While some outside advisers warned against centering the fight against Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” on Medicaid cuts — dismissing them as only about poor people, according to a person briefed on the conversations — Jeffries said he was sure that was the way to go. And at the end of last year, he again pushed to focus the Democrats’ message on the lapsed healthcare subsidies, leading to a government shutdown. He felt the weight of what he was doing and how it might go wrong, at one point calling aides from the airport, stressing about whether he should return to the Capitol. “He’s just really good at being in the moment, not making decisions before he needs to. And then once he makes it, he’s prepared to go and doesn’t allow himself or others to be distracted,” said Rep. Joe Morelle, a close ally in the caucus and the lieutenant he dispatched to work on retaliatory gerrymandering in their home state of New York. Al Sharpton has known the president going back to New York in the 1980s. He has also been a Jeffries friend and political ally for 30 years. “He’s the same Hakeem, except better at it,” Sharpton said. Sharpton broke into a broad smile when imagining what the Trump-Jeffries dynamic will look like. “Trump will be in the awkward position of meeting with a Black guy smarter than him,” Sharpton said. “The question is whether he’s been so humiliated by this defeat that he’ll just have to take it.” Read that quote, Jeffries smiled and did not dispute it. Many on the left dislike Jeffries — and he knows Some Democrats are already arguing that Jeffries isn’t bold enough, that he won’t bring down the hammer on Trump or Democrats who defect. Jeffries has remained a prime focus for the left — some because of his cautious resistance to their causes, particularly on his support for Israel; some irritated over his snapping back at critics, some noting his outreach to Republicans like Jared Kushner. A Change.org petition that declares Jeffries “simply not the right choice” for speaker has racked up a million signatures since it was launched in September. Popular radio host Charlamagne tha God turned Jeffries’ well-known love of hip-hop against him with the nickname “AIPAC Shakur.” In September, Palestinian journalist and author Rula Jebreal called him an “AIPAC monkey” and an “errand boy,” comments widely condemned as racist for which she later apologized. Jeffries almost faced a primary this year from Chi Ossé, the city councilman from Brooklyn who argued top Democrats had failed to respond effectively to Trump or to provide leadership for the party. While Jeffries tends to avoid responding to critics, talk of a primary challenge led his political operation to declare, “If Team Gentrification wants a primary fight, our response will be forceful and unrelenting.” Ossé didn’t run after being pushed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to stand down, though he picked up the charge on Wednesday morning, mocking Jeffries for saying the wins were about America and not about Democrats — a post that was boosted by the Sen. Bernie Sanders-inspired group Our Revolution. Earlier this year, as a picture of Jeffries flashed on the screen at the primary victory party for Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, the crowd chanted, “You’re next!” “It was very interesting to me, as observed by others,” Jeffries told CNN, “that there was almost zero diversity in that crowd.” Jeffries pays attention to loyalty and trust. He values those who didn’t start paying attention to him when he was already en route to being a big deal. He is deferential to elders in politics, especially in the Congressional Black Caucus, and after growing up working class and representing one of the poorer and most Black districts in the country, he dismisses those he sees as newcomers to the cause. He took a different approach to the incoming members themselves, working with even the socialists who blasted him in their campaigns over the summer and fall. Among his most useful allies is former President Barack Obama, whom Jeffries endorsed for president in 2008 over then-New York Sen. Hillary Clinton — something that nearly led to Jeffries’ excommunication from local political circles. Over phone calls and regular meetings at Obama’s Washington office, the former president has been impressed by Jeffries’ message discipline and his ruthlessness leading the efforts to fight back on gerrymandering. Obama is closer in age to Jeffries, and while he worked closely with Pelosi, an adviser told CNN, he sees the incoming speaker as the next generation taking the baton. Former presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton called on Wednesday too, offering to help. So did a few of the candidates likely gearing up to run for the White House in 2028. Some have yet to commit to backing Jeffries for speaker, though the size of his majority — potentially approaching 260 members — makes a few holdouts moot. Underscoring the breadth of his support, Michigan Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the climate activist group Sunrise Movement and a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, now plans to vote for Jeffries, reversing his position earlier in the campaign. Sunrise has promoted primary challenges against Democratic incumbents over their support for Israel. “It’s all just a question of what your leverage is at any given time. And there are times when we are having these debates within the party, and there’s times to come together with unity to focus on the bigger task,” Lawrence said. Lawrence was asked how he reconciled the corporate PAC money Jeffries raised in the midterms with his own demand to get all corporate money out of politics. “Politics is full of contradictions,” Lawrence responded. Inscrutable by design Jeffries started Tuesday in New York and traveled to DC for lunch with party officials — eating at the same crab shack where Democrats dined on midterm day in 2018, when they flipped the House in Trump’s first term. When he went before the cameras in Washington to claim victory on Tuesday night, he switched his walk-on music to another favorite: the Notorious B.I.G.’s “Unbelievable.” But Jeffries is so private that aides and colleagues sometimes joke that he doesn’t even want them to know where he lives, or what exactly he does when he sometimes holes up by himself in big moments. His own account of his phone call with his mother on Tuesday night: “She said, ‘Love you and proud of you.’” Pushed to elaborate, he would only say, “We had a longer conversation, but that was the gist.” Ask members of Congress who consider themselves close to him for their favorite Jeffries story and they struggle to come up with specifics, though they gush about how much they like and trust him. “I call him ‘Silk’ because he’s so smooth,” said his close ally New York Rep. Greg Meeks, who variously compared him to a chess player, famed Yankees closer Mariano Rivera, and in terms of tuning out the noise to focus on the mission, Martin Luther King Jr. In a politics that has become a running soap opera, Jeffries is determined to remain more of an enigma in public than a character — though he also rejects that he is an enigma. “Seems to me that there’s nobody in the district that I represent currently or in the district that I previously represented in the assembly thinks that I’m introverted,” Jeffries said. “At the end of the day, we’re a team within the House Democratic caucus in the Congress. It’s an honor to be the quarterback of that team. But we have to remain focused on actually winning for the American people. And we do that together.” Sitting in Puerto Rico, pressed by CNN to describe how he felt himself about the wins, the arc that got him there, the history-making he’s about to do, Jeffries finally relented. “You never thought that hip-hop would take it this far,” he said, quoting a different Biggie Smalls song, “Juicy.” That’s it? “That’s it,” he said. “That says a lot, means a lot to me — without saying a whole lot.”

bbc.com.title: Trump says he was 'kidding' about Dana White press secretary offer
bbc.com.text:
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he "was kidding" about asking Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be the White House press secretary.
Trump told the media on Sunday that White "loves the idea" but that the invitation was "just a little fun".
It comes after the president posted on his Truth Social platform on Saturday that he had offered White the role, asking him to take it while writing, "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other."
White said later that day he was going to meet the president on Monday, but would not be drawn into whether or not he would take the vacant position.
On Sunday Trump told reporters White was visiting him on Monday for "other reasons".
"I think he's going to be in Washington. So he's going to come over and see me.
"I will tell you, I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea. And there's only one Dana. He's great," the president said.
"But, it was it was just a little fun."
The press secretary role is yet to be filled after it became vacant in October when Katie Zacharia quit after less than five days in the job.
She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who was the youngest press secretary in US history and had held the role since Trump began his second term.
Trump's job offer came after a heavy loss in the midterm elections, where the Republican Party lost its majority in both houses of Congress.
In his Truth Social post on Saturday, he said he was "pleased to announce" that White "has been offered the job".
He said he had asked White to bring with him several current and former mixed martial arts fighters as "assistants".
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," he wrote.
"Dana, please take the job!"
Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference on Saturday, the UFC chief executive said he had "lot of jobs already".
"I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he said of their planned Monday meeting, but did not say whether or not he would take the job.
White leads UFC, and PowerSlap , a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, as well as recently launching promotion company Zuffa Boxing.
He is also a board member of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
White appeared as a speaker in support of Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.
This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.

bbc.com.title: At least 34 dead after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
bbc.com.text:
- Published
At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.
The Interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.
Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
The Canary Islands have become a major entry point into Europe for migrants and refugees making the dangerous Atlantic crossing from West Africa.
The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.
Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

bbc.com.title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow and his parents and sister at their home has died in hospital, Polish police say.
The 24-year-old, who officials said was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies", was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
Krakow police said the suspected gunman died early on Monday morning.
After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man but did not confirm his name.
In the hours after the shooting, a minister said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.
Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.
On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.
Speaking on Sunday, one of the two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.
The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers.
Professor Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible."
"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."
Pędziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.
On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.
Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded.
Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".
She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside.
Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".
"I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said.
In the wake of the shooting, Poland declared the country would enter two days of national mourning.
After travelling to Krakow, Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków".
"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.
Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

bbc.com.title: What do we know about Nvidia CEO’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy?
bbc.com.text:
What do we know about Nvidia CEO’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy?
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its boss Jensen Huang had a relationship with businesswoman Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Huang has been in charge of the tech giant for 30 years, and is a popular public figure - but will this scandal hurt his reputation? The BBC’s Steve Lai explains everything you need to know.

bbc.com.title: Jensen Huang: Why a personal scandal for the face of the AI boom has provoked a national security scare
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Jensen Huang is one of the technology industry's most high-profile figures.
He rose to prominence as the business he leads - artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia - became one of the world's most valuable companies.
As the face of the AI boom, Huang also became close to Donald Trump as the president pushed for the US to keep its dominance of the technology over China.
The 63-year-old who was once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" and referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan is now mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US.
He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine - a biography on Huang, tells the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.
Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.
"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".
Huang has long found himself at the centre of US-China tensions. Trump has repeatedly said the two nations are in a race for dominance.
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.
The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.
Since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.
But it means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. In recent years Huang has engaged in a flurry of shuttle diplomacy, dashing between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.
Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.
Quarter after quarter of late, Nvidia has been locked out of that lucrative market. Despite his ostensible closeness to Trump, Huang has not managed to wrest this concession from the administration.
Huang founded Nvidia with fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993.
The company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.
Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates.
"In 2012 these machine learning neural net researchers started to use it for that purpose and Jensen immediately recognised that this was going to be a massive industry and the future of computing. He began to pour enormous amounts of resources into building what was essentially the AI hardware market," says Witt.
"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them."
Nvidia is now worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.
"The first real neural net of modern times on an Nvidia network was Alex Krizhevsky's Alexnet and they trained that on two Nvidia cards in Alex's bedroom. Now we do the same thing but we do it with 200,000 - 300,000 cards and instead of doing it in a bedroom we do it in a giant barn full of computers called a data centre," adds Witt.
"So when you think about a data centre buildout, when you hear the AI infrastructure buildout, Jensen runs a tollbooth. All of that goes through him. And it made his company at least temporarily, the most valuable company in the world."
Nvidia's board has announced a probe following reports by the New York Times that Huang had engaged in a romantic relationship with a woman believed by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.
For now, though, Nvidia's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".
Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is also no clear successor to the 63-year old tech boss.
Who is Huang's wife?
Huang met his wife Lori at Oregon State University, where she was also studying electrical engineering and was his lab partner.
They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.
He has credited Lori and Madison for making black leather jackets his signature style.
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.
The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.
"Jensen in my conversations with him and in other conversations has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man. That's very important to him," says Witt.
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways. Both of his children work for Nvidia. Spencer and Maddison. The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
Huang for his part released a statement which said, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
What do we know about the affair?
US officials had concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reports.
She was a top executive at Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.
"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.
Additional reporting by Ayeshea Perera in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

bbc.com.title: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence
Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.
It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.
"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.
The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.
One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.
What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.
Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.
Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.
The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.
While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.
After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.
We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.
We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.
The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.
DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.
The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.
Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.
In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.
France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.
The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.
Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.
DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.
We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.
They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.
And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.
Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.
Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.
But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.
"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."
Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."
Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.
That area was Quartier Nord.
Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.
Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.
Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.
"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.
It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.
"Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."
Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.
Money is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.
In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.
Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.
The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members.
"They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains.
"You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."
Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."
DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.
He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders.
"People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."
During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".
"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
We challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.
He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets.
"If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.
Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".
At a so-called deal point in a social housing estate - sealed off and controlled by DZ Mafia - price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana are graffitied on a wall.
The estate acts as a natural fortress for drug dealers. With one major road in and out, they can control the flow of customers and see if the police are coming.
It is not uncommon for the sound of automatic gunfire to fill the night air in these areas.
After months of negotiations, a deal-point manager from a rival gang agrees to meet us where he works.
