In an interview on the CBS network’s 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, the president acknowledged that the aggressive crackdown had hurt him politically and said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.
Trump was asked by the 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether his deportation policy had gone too far. “I think it was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”
The president’s comments were an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.
Since Trump returned to office, sweeping Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids at workplaces, homes and public spaces have ensnared people with no criminal records, separated families and spread fear in immigrant communities. Federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during operations in Minneapolis this year.
The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”
Trump added that there were competing views within the country about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported or allowed to remain if they were working and paying taxes. He said some people believed that “they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company” and “in some cases, paying taxes”.
Trump said he believed an agreement with Democrats was achievable, allowing some long-term undocumented residents to stay while continuing to remove people convicted of serious crimes. He proposed targeting killers, rapists and drug dealers while making an accommodation for people who had been in the country for 10 or 15 years.
“Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said. He described the proposal as something that could be negotiated, saying: “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”
Trump suggested Democrats were receptive to a compromise, saying some had already contacted him. Asked whether he could refrain from name-calling for six months to secure an agreement, he replied: “Very easily.”
Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat, agreeing with an assessment by his vice-president, JD Vance, that the conflict had been a significant factor. He also cited what he described as growing dislike of Israel.
He maintained, however, that the military campaign had been justified and said he would make the same decision again. “My answer is an emphatic yes because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Trump insisted the war had been won and predicted that Tehran would eventually negotiate a deal. He acknowledged that the military campaign might not have been popular in the short term, saying: “I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.”
He said he was not looking to escalate the conflict after the midterms.
In a separate interview with CNN, the president said a renewed assault on Iran was “highly unlikely” but warned that his decision “depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement”.
On the economy, the president conceded that his administration had failed to communicate its achievements effectively, despite repeatedly claiming that employment, investment and stock market figures were at record levels. “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me,” he said.
Trump signalled an openness to safeguards for artificial intelligence, despite having previously favoured allowing technology companies to police themselves rather than imposing sweeping government restrictions. “I don’t mind guardrails,” he told 60 Minutes. “But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position.”
The interview also raised questions about the substantial increase in Trump’s personal wealth since his return to the White House.
Douthat cited a Forbes estimate that Trump’s net worth had increased by $3bn from the autumn of 2024 to the autumn of 2025. Trump initially suggested that the increase reflected the general performance of the stock market and said his finances were managed by his son.
Asked about his family’s cryptocurrency business, World Liberty Financial, in which he is a co-owner and which has attracted investment from people connected to the United Arab Emirates, Trump defended the arrangement by saying: “I know nothing about it.”
But Dan Alexander, a Forbes senior editor who calculates the net worth of wealthy individuals for the magazine, challenged Trump’s explanation in a lengthy thread on X, arguing that the president’s increased fortune could not be explained simply by stock market gains.
Alexander identified several sources including cryptocurrency ventures that generated more than $1bn in proceeds and the appreciation of tokens retained by Trump, overseas licensing agreements that expanded the value of his branding business, and the removal of an almost $500m financial penalty in his New York civil fraud case.
Trump also offered a glimpse of the Republican succession battle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, saying he might endorse a candidate but had not decided whether to intervene. Asked whether he expected to endorse a successor, Trump replied: “Probably. Not necessarily.”
He described the Republican party as having a strong field of potential candidates and praised secretary of state Marco Rubio while declining to rule out other contenders.
The president said his endorsement would carry considerable weight but suggested he might be better off staying out of the contest. He also expressed confidence that the “Make America great again” movement could survive without him as its leader, describing its defining principles as strong borders and a strong military.
At the end of the interview, Trump was asked whether he could forgive political opponents including former FBI director James Comey and former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, even before the judgment of God. Trump said: “The answer is no. I want to be honest, no.”
Douthat followed up: “Mr President. You have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime, and you are telling me that before the judgment throne of God you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies? After all that’s been given to you? Come on, help me out here.”
But Trump remained adamant: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”
Douthat noted that many presidents were remembered with a single line, such as “He freed the slaves” or “He won the cold war”, and asked what line would Trump’s presidency be remembered with.
The president said: “That I made America great again.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world
theguardian.com.text:
In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse
theguardian.com.text:
When Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.
“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.
Andy Burnham expressed concern over the development weeks before he became prime minister, and Bev Craig, his successor as Greater Manchester mayor, said she too was concerned. “Old industry wouldn’t have got that close to your house,” she said. “So why is it that new industry can?”
This week, villagers will attempt to block plans by Whistl, the distribution firm that operates the warehouse, to use dozens of HGVs and trailers for its round-the-clock operation. In a two-day public inquiry, they will describe how the “cacophony” of noise is already driving some to sleep deprivation and depression.
“It’s had a profound impact on the neighbourhood,” said Retford, a burly man with a booming voice who after so many years in the police is not easily shaken. “The noise wakes you up at 2am and you can’t get back to sleep. We’ve not had a proper night’s sleep in well over a year. It’s a living hell.”
This once-quiet village is now on the frontline in a nationwide fightback against superstructures springing up everywhere from Devon to Cardiff and the Scottish Borders. Plans were announced last week for Britain’s largest datacentre at the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire, and a further 315 “hyperscale” datacentres are queueing to connect to the National Grid.
Down the road from Retford’s house, a woman looked out of her daughter’s bedroom window at the Whistl warehouse just metres away. The woman, a police officer who does not want to be named, said her 10-year-old son, who is autistic, refused to play in the garden because of the “continuously whirring” noise of the conveyor belts. Her eight-year-old daughter has become too scared to play in her bedroom.
“As soon as she comes home from school, those blinds will be shut because she doesn’t want anyone to see in,” she said, pointing to a CCTV camera on the warehouse facing their home. “She hates it. She does get scared about it.”
Like many of their neighbours, the woman and her husband moved to Astley before plans had been submitted by a firm part-owned by Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, run by the billionaire John Whittaker.
Back then, they were surrounded by farmland where lambs, cows and horses grazed. Now their view is a giant hunk of grey steel that was named the worst new building in the UK this year. “It was a lovely view, so secluded,” she said. “When we saw the structure of this, it was like: oh my God, what is this?”
As mayor, Burnham said earlier this year that the development had not been managed properly and that key things “should have been done differently”. Wigan council said it acted properly in approving the superstructure despite objections from the local MP and dozens of residents. However, the council’s leader, Labour’s Nazia Rehman, admitted last month that “some lessons have been learned” and said that in future “consultations [with residents] will be proactive”. Local leaders have scrapped plans for four other giant warehouses in response to the backlash.
Helen Halbous, who moved to the estate seven years ago, said: “It’s a feeling of being screwed over by Wigan council, having been born and brought up here. People who had a voice of power [in the council] either made this awful decision or they looked away and let it happen. It was a little mining village and now we’re this industrial centre. It’s so wrong.”
Halbous, 47, said she and her partner, Sami Halbous, now felt trapped in a house they once loved and they feared they would be unable to sell up. “A neighbour had their home valued and they lost 30%, and that’s if they can sell,” she said.
Residents felt hoodwinked about the size of the structure and its closeness to their homes, Halbous said. “The plan in 2019 was it was to be used for employment. It was never to have an 18-metre-high warehouse. Those permissions were changed [before 2024] and changed really quietly. We wouldn’t have bought here and let ourselves get trapped like this.”
PLP, the land owner, said the size and scale of the buildings had not changed since its planning application in 2023. It said earlier plans for smaller units, submitted in 2017 by Peel, one of its biggest shareholders, had since lapsed.
Wigan council said it recognised the “strength of feeling in the community and do not underestimate the impact residents tell us the development has had on them”. It said an independent review found its planning process was “legally sound” and followed national guidelines but there were “lessons around engagement and transparency”. It said: “We have acknowledged those findings and have taken steps to improve our approach.”
Whistl, which began operating at the site in July, has responded to the concerns by promising to use quieter vehicles and stopping their use outside between midnight and 6am. The firm said it took residents’ concerns seriously and was “committed to meeting its licensing responsibilities and being a good neighbour”. A Whistl spokesperson said the noise mitigation measures would remain in place and the overnight pause on activity in the yard would continue while all parties tried to “identify a sustainable, long-term solution”.
Retford became so fed up with the disturbance that he began overnight observations to track the big vehicles clanking around near his home. He commissioned independent acoustics experts to produce a sound report, convinced that the “cacophony of rolling thunder, a booming sound”, breached regulations.
A fightback fund launched by residents has so far raised £78,000, much of which will be spent on lawyers for next week’s public inquiry.
For Retford and his wife, Carole, 71, the impact has been huge. “Bloody hell, there’s not a lot of things I’ve not seen in my life,” he said. “I don’t get easily shocked and I’m not a flaky character, but this has had a profound effect on me. We’re not fuddy-duddies or nimbies. This is big business riding over the little people like us, saying ‘screw the lot of you’.”
Retford and his wife have spoken to their doctor about sleep deprivation. “It’s a torture for a very good reason, because it just drains you – and that is the effect it’s having on us,” he said.
Carole became close to tears. Staring up at the warehouse, she said: “It’s changed our lives. Your moods go up and down to being very depressed and very emotional about it because there’s no way out at the minute. People use the ‘depression’ word too lightly, but if you feel there’s no way out, it does get to you.”

theguardian.com.title: Kraków shooting suspect who killed six has died, say police in Poland
theguardian.com.text:
A gunman suspected of killing six people in a popular market square in Kraków has died in hospital, Polish police said early on Monday.
The suspect, a 24-year-old named in local media as Michal O, who authorities say was probably inspired by far-right ideologies, had been wounded in a shootout with police and had been in critical condition in hospital.
“We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Malopolska Policja wrote on X.
Polish prosecutors had opened a terrorism investigation after the man opened fire on Saturday afternoon, killing six including a Briton and injuring 17, in an attack that shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its European neighbours.
Karolina Galecka, an interior ministry spokeswoman, told radio TOK FM on Monday: “There were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that have been partially examined and interpreted.
“These patches were associated with various motifs that are currently being analysed by specialists,” she added, declining to comment further as the investigation was ongoing.
Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home after the attack were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.
Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police officers were also among the injured, one of whom was in a serious condition.
As two days of national mourning began, the national prosecutor’s office said on social media it had launched an investigation into “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.
The rare mass shooting has deepened concern about extremism in Poland after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.
The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.
The Kraków suspect drove into the city’s main square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, at top speed at about 3pm on Saturday. Wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, he started shooting at random as he took what the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło described as a “wild ride” around the square.

theguardian.com.title: Fixing UK’s youth jobs crisis demands much more investment, TUC boss warns
theguardian.com.text:
Fixing Britain’s youth jobs crisis will require ministers to drastically increase investment in employment support while avoiding arbitrary cuts to benefits, the head of the trade union movement has said.
Before an important official report expected next week, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said the government had a “once in a generation chance” to secure young people’s futures.
In an interview with the Guardian before the highly anticipated Milburn review into young people and work, he said the costs of increasing job support, education and training would be outweighed by economic gains that would help to ease the pressure on the welfare state.
“There is no solution that is cost-free,” he said. “The government is going to have to be prepared to invest in securing the future of those young people, but also to invest to secure what is the future of our economy.
“This is where the government is going to have to be clear. Of course as a country it’s right to invest in our physical infrastructure, but also we have to invest in social infrastructure too.”
Ministers are braced for the report by Alan Milburn, the former Labour health secretary, to recommend welfare cuts to fund job support for almost a million young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).
The report was delayed until after the budget amid fears that the call for welfare cuts would sit uneasily alongside the tax and spending plans of the chancellor, John Healey.
Andy Burnham has said the surge in young people who are Neet is an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” and that tougher benefits rules and more help for young people will form part of his government’s response to the Milburn report.
The prime minister has been at pains to take a cautious approach to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion, which forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn on planned disability benefit cuts within a year of coming to power.
Calling on Burnham to focus on delivering a step change in employment support, Nowak said increased investment would help to bring down the benefits bill by getting more young people into work.
“We can’t afford to not do this stuff, as the benefits bill will go up if young people are not supported,” he said.
“I don’t think this government is going to repeat the mistake of the previous attempt at benefit reform, where you make arbitrary cuts, [and] where you have an impact on some of the most vulnerable people without thinking about how you support people into work.”
There is rising concern over youth worklessness. Most Britons now see the youth jobs crisis as one of the biggest problems facing the country – ranking it second only to the cost of living and above NHS waiting lists, housing, crime and immigration, according to polling by the research company Focaldata for the Jobs Foundation.
The employment charity, co-founded by the Conservative peer Matthew Elliott, is behind a national campaign to tackle worklessness that launches on Monday. It includes a pledge, backed by a group of leading employers – including Amazon, Pret a Manger, NatWest, Marks & Spencer and Shell – that have committed to support young people who have been overlooked for work.
A government spokesperson said: “We are determined to turn the tide on youth unemployment which has been years in the making.
“We have already pledged £2.5bn in youth employment support, which will deliver almost 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn, while engaging with business including some of Britain’s biggest retail and hospitality brands to create up to 200,000 jobs for young people.
“Further reform will follow the Milburn review, which will be published in the autumn.”

theguardian.com.title: Stop undermining Jim Chalmers, environment minister urges Labor colleagues
theguardian.com.text:
The environment minister, Murray Watt, has urged ministers to stop undermining the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, as Labor struggles to sell its budget and looks to cut popular clean energy subsidies to help with the fight against inflation.
Cabinet ministers met again on Monday to discuss potential budget savings to be included in next month’s mid-year update, part of efforts to reducing spending to ease pressure on the economy.
Watt was asked about speculation of tension between the treasurer and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and whether he’d like to see an end to “undermining and leaking” against Chalmers.
“Yes, I would,” Watt said. “As a member of the government, I take seriously the responsibility to work together to support government policies and also to get our work to support each other in what are very difficult times.
“I think that Jim Chalmers is doing an excellent job as a treasurer in what are very difficult economic times; many of the features that are impacting on our economy are sort of well outside any treasurer’s control, and I very much support Jim Chalmers in his efforts.”
Watt conceded Chalmers was being undermined from within Labor.
“It’s pretty obvious that there are all sorts of people making all sorts of comments.”
A new round of opinion polls added to Labor’s political pain on Monday, with the Resolve Political Monitor in the Age and Sydney Morning Herald showing Labor’s primary vote falling to 28 percentage points, down from 34.6% at last year’s election.
The Coalition also dropped one point to 22%, while One Nation was steady at 25%.
A Redbridge poll in the Financial Review showed Labor’s primary vote slipped two percentage points to 26%, while the Coalition’s jumped four points to 25%. One Nation was down one point to 28%.
Monday’s meeting of the expenditure review committee of cabinet comes after last week’s interest rate hike from the Reserve Bank. The governor, Michele Bullock, said while it is up to governments to manage their budgets independently of the RBA, public and private spending had caused “excess demand” in the economy.
Watt accused the Coalition and minor parties of leaving existing spending proposals to linger in parliament, including savings from changes to the private health insurance rebate for over 65s.
“Let’s not forget that for all of their demands that we find more savings, the Coalition currently are blocking the government from saving $10 billion in measures that are before the parliament,” Watt said.
Albanese has confirmed spending in the public service will be scrutinised as the government looks for savings in the budget update, expected in the middle of December. Last year, departments and agencies were asked to identify potential savings of as much as 5% from their annual budgets, part of the government’s efforts to cut lower-priority spending.
Spending on Labor’s $7bn home battery subsidy program and incentives for electric vehicle purchases could be reined in.
Announced in April 2025, the batteries program was originally designed to cost about $2bn. More than 600,000 systems have been installed, but the program could have means testing rules added.
Separately, subsidies designed to promote uptake of electric vehicles has cost the budget far more than originally anticipated.
Angus Taylor announced an opposition “red tape razor gang” on Monday, designed to reduce the burden on business from costly regulation.

theguardian.com.title: Burnham’s homelessness pledge to ‘get everyone in for Christmas’ in jeopardy
theguardian.com.text:
Andy Burnham’s pledge to tackle rough sleeping by getting “everyone in for Christmas” is in jeopardy amid rising numbers of people on the streets and a severe housing shortage.
Official figures show an increase of nearly 1,000 people sleeping rough in England between January and June, the latest month for which figures are available.
There were 8,748 rough sleepers in England in June, the highest number since November 2025, according to government statistics.
Only 15% of those were found accommodation by the end of June, the lowest level since August 2025 as councils struggle with the growing demand for temporary and affordable housing.
The homelessness minister, Florence Eshalomi, said the government hoped to offer a bed to every rough sleeper by Christmas but that there was a chronic shortage of suitable housing.
Asked whether every person on the streets in England would be offered accommodation in the next six weeks, she said: “We’re hoping to offer that, but what we are definitely offering is a route off the street for everyone who wants to take up that offer.”
A “route off the street” may not necessarily involve housing, Eshalomi said.
“For some people it will be a route into accommodation, for some people it could be a … dedicated plan around their mental health or substance misuse, so that’s what we are committed to.
“The offer of a bed will be there for people who want that. We cannot force people off the streets – we’ve got to respect that as well – but that offer will be there.”
Burnham has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership.
Councils across England have said the number of homeless families is growing as a result of the chronic shortage of affordable housing, record demand for temporary accommodation and the long-term freeze of local housing allowance, meaning rents far outstrip the welfare available to those on low incomes.
Frontline professionals are also concerned about the impact of the prisons early release scheme, with some offenders being released without stable accommodation, as well as a flood of no-fault evictions before the practice was banned on 1 May.
A record 135,600 households in England were living in temporary accommodation such as B&Bs and hostels at the end of March 2026, according to official figures. This is about 90% higher than a decade ago and 4% higher than the previous year.
In a speech in Downing Street when he became prime minister on 20 July, Burnham said: “I will soon go through that door behind me and issue my first instruction: to end rough sleeping in our country.”
The next month, he announced increased funding of £442m as part of what he called the “national drive to get everyone in for Christmas”.
In October he set out a further £432m in funding from March 2027 so that people would be “offered a safe route off the streets this winter” and support to the end of this parliament.
Eshalomi, who was appointed by Burnham in July, previously described the freeze of local housing allowance as one of the “systemic barriers” and a “big sticking point” in reducing homelessness.
Speaking on a visit to a temporary accommodation facility in Manchester last week, she said the area was not “best policy” and that she raised it “constantly with colleagues … with the Treasury”.
Asked whether she raised it with fellow ministers before John Healey’s budget last month, she said: “I’ve been an MP since 2019. I’ve been raising it since then.”
Eshalomi said she was working with councils and housing associations in England to bring thousands of empty or derelict properties into use to help tackle rough sleeping.
She said ultimately the solution was “building those homes”.
“It’s around making sure we’re building more social and affordable homes so that people don’t have to find themselves choosing between not having enough money and support to live in a private rented sector.”

theguardian.com.title: Starbucks plans to hire 7,500 staff in major UK expansion plan
theguardian.com.text:
Starbucks has set out plans to hire 7,500 new baristas over the next five years, in a boost to youth employment as the chain pins hopes for future growth on the north of the country.
The US coffee shop chain, which employs more than 18,000 people in the UK, said the hiring spree would focus on the Midlands, north of England, Wales and Scotland, as it targets growth north of the M25.
The roles are expected to staff 500 new coffee shops which Starbucks hopes to open across the country by 2031. The company set out the growth plan earlier this year after shutting dozens of underperforming outlets in Britain last year as part of a $1bn (£750m) global restructuring.
Darren King, who runs Starbucks UK, said: “We’re deeply focused on how we can help more young people into these positions, starting by making entry-level roles as accessible as possible.”
Starbucks is a large youth employer and set out its plan before an official report into the number of young people not in education, employment or training, known as Neets, which hit a record high above 1 million at the start of the year.
The rise in worklessness was dealt a blow in the run-up to the budget last month, as UK employers cut back on hiring amid worries about rising costs and the outlook for the British economy, according to a monthly survey.
The number of people taking up permanent jobs across the UK fell for the first time in four months, according to the latest jobs report from KPMG and the Recruitment & Employment Confederation, compiled by S&P Global. Recruitment for temporary roles also fell, for the first time since March.
Jon Holt, the chief executive and UK senior partner of KPMG, said: “October saw employers pull back on hiring in the month leading up to the budget, ending a run of more positive news over recent months. Renewed geopolitical and economic uncertainty weighed on confidence, with further energy price shocks and a global bond sell-off pushing borrowing costs higher.”
Holt added: “Businesses will now be assessing whether the measures announced in the budget give them enough stability to absorb the external pressures and higher costs they face. But with the Bank of England increasing interest rates and inflation set to continue rising over the coming months, there is a risk the green shoots we had been seeing in the jobs market could stall.”
Separate analysis by the Resolution Foundation found that job satisfaction among UK workers is at a record low, amid a lack of flexible working, insecure jobs and a loss of independence.

theguardian.com.title: Victorian election 2026: Concern and scepticism among Labor MPs as new poll shows party trailing One Nation
theguardian.com.text:
Victorian Labor MPs are both sceptical and seriously concerned about a new poll ahead of the state election showing the party trailing third behind One Nation, with its primary vote at an all-time low of just 18%.
The DemosAU/PremierNational, first published by the Herald Sun on Monday, showed Labor’s primary vote share has crashed seven points to 18%, putting it in third place behind the Coalition’s 33% and One Nation’s 21%. At the same time, the Greens improved their primary vote to 17%, an increase of three points since September.
It means the Coalition now leads Labor on a two-party preferred basis 56-44, compared with 52-48 in September.
George Hasanakos, DemosAU’s head of research, said if the poll were replicated on election night then many contests across the state would be between the Liberals or Nationals and One Nation, which would then result in a “clear Coalition majority”.
“If that happens, One Nation has to poll really, really well to have a chance of winning, because Labor and Greens preferences will flow to the Liberals,” he said.
On election night, the Victorian Electoral Commission plans to conduct a two-candidate-preferred count, or 2CP, between the two candidates it expects to finish with the most support after preferences are distributed. The commission is selecting the indicative 2CP for each seat based on polling, analysis of preference flows and results from previous elections. It will not publish the indicative 2CPs before election day to avoid influencing voter behaviour.
Hasanakos added that he “double, triple, quadruple checked” the result of the “extraordinary” poll, which had 1,562 respondents, an effective sample of 818 and a margin of error of 3.4%.
“We went to the trouble of a bigger sample here, and I stand by it,” he said.
Ben Carroll repeatedly refused to say whether he was worried about the poll at a press conference in South Melbourne on Monday morning.
“What I’m focused on every day is fighting for working people and making sure that every Victorian that goes into the ballot on November 28 knows that under my government you have a government on your side that will fight for you,” he told reporters.
“The alternative is a Liberal-One Nation government that will fight against you – they’re going to shrink the economy, cause a recession and make life difficult for every single Victorian.”
But the result has sparked serious concerns among the Labor caucus, even though some MPs are sceptical about the 18% figure. Inside Labor’s campaign headquarters, they are treating the result as an “outlier” and point to other public polls that have their primary vote in the 20s.
Several Labor MPs, unauthorised to speak publicly, have told Guardian Australia there are many in the caucus questioning their party’s strategy.
This includes a focus in recent days on crime – an issue that is typically a Coalition strength. On Sunday, Carroll announced a $204m plan to enable judges to sentence low- and mid-level youth offenders to a new rehabilitation detention program, while on Monday he announced $70m to recruit 200 more police reservists to reopen stations and build and upgrade more stations.
“Caucus is really angry and deflated, because this is all happening because of him,” one MP said.
“Even if it’s higher than 18, and we get back into something with a two in front of it, the experiment has been an epic fail, the campaign is in freefall, and it’s about to get a whole lot worse.”
Another MP said the focus on crime was “diabolically stupid strategy” as the government had years to tackle community concern around rising rates.
The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Monday said her party had a focus on “getting tough on crime”, including by introducing Aidan’s Law to toughen sentencing for attacks on people who step in to protect others.
Carroll immediately matched the commitment to introduce the proposed law, named after 22-year-old Aidan Becker, who was fatally stabbed at Mernda station after stepping in to protect a 14-year-old during an alleged violent robbery.
It comes as Pauline Hanson rejected reports by the Age and 60 Minutes on Sunday that her former national campaign director Sean Black continues to secretly work for One Nation in Victoria.
Black in 2018 was jailed for rape and subsequently lost his appeal against the conviction but was then rehired by One Nation in 2020 as a campaign director after serving his time. Hanson sacked him after political pressure earlier this year.
She told the Australian Financial Review on Monday “the day that I sacked him [Sean Black] that was the day he finished up”.

theguardian.com.title: CFMEU ‘enjoy a significant level of influence’ over Victorian government, Big Build royal commission hears
theguardian.com.text:
The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian Big Build projects has heard a major construction company feared putting the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) offside because of its close links to the Daniel Andrews Labor government.
The first block of hearings under the commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria will hear evidence about the union’s involvement in a level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury, north of Melbourne, in 2022.
The project involved the removal of a level crossing and the construction of a new rail bridge and underpass.
The counsel assisting the commission, Chris Young KC, said 20 witnesses have been compelled to appear during the November hearings.
But he warned that others were not complying with orders to produce documents to the commission, including using the excuse of “government policy” to delay their production. Failing to comply with such orders is a criminal offence.
“It is extremely concerning that some parties have not complied with the terms of those notices to produce,” Young said.
The hearings in November will focus on what government officials did during a June 2022 meeting in order to appease the union, who had forced work to stop on the Gap Road project.
Young showed the commission evidence that – in the years before the union interfered in the project – there was increasing awareness within the construction sector about the prospect of industrial action curtailing work, and the growing influence of the CFMEU.
He said that in 2017, one of the companies involved in the Gap Road project, John Holland, noted that the CFMEU was “proud of the fact that none of their site visits are code compliant”.
It also noted in an email the “significance of the CFMEU relationship with the Andrews government in Victoria, and the impact this is having, and will have in the future, in respect of client relationships with the Victorian government”.
Such was the extent of that relationship that John Holland officials suspected the CFMEU would have a “substantial amount of knowledge around proposed government tenders and input” in respect of the tender process.
“We are thus particularly mindful of the optics in our interactions with union stakeholders,” the 2017 email said.
Four years later, the construction company noted that “the CFMEU are emboldened by their success on major infrastructure projects,” and later in 2021, that they “enjoy a significant level of influence within the state government”.
“It is a level of influence not seen in previous years and is unlikely to diminish.”
Police called to dispute
Young told the hearing that four of the CFMEU officials who would later force work to stop at Gap Road had similarly interfered in the Metro Tunnel project.
He said the officials entered the Gap Road project’s eastern portal 29 times in January 2020, and were involved in activity considered to be unlawful, but nonetheless received attention from the government, which asked if the safety issues they raised were valid.
Young said that a “very high risk rating” was applied to the possibility of industrial action on Gap Road.
But he said that it was not until May 2022 where this risk escalated, and CFMEU officials more regularly appeared on site.
By early June, the health and safety manager for the Rail Network Alliance involved in the project, Neil Thompson, was calling police, desperate for their help in removing union officials who were stopping work including by sitting on barriers and refusing to move.
Young tendered internal notes taken on the union activity that showed there were references to the CFMEU officials warning workers that “you guys better not turn up tonight otherwise we will smash you during the day,” and that “their life would be [made] very difficult for them personally” if they continued working on the project.
A recording of a phone call between Thompson and WorkSafe and a subsequent email showed that on 6 June – the day before a meeting that is central to the commission’s hearings – he was unclear about how to get work to continue on site.
Thompson stressed the need for the union to be removed, given trains had been stopped on the line in order for a bridge to be built.
“We actually called Victoria police to escort themself off site,” Thompson said in the call to WorkSafe.
“Victoria police said there was nothing they could do. We’re going around in circles a bit because last week WorkSafe said there was nothing they could do.
“We’re just having to put up with no work happening at the moment.”
The following day, Young said, there was a 13-minute meeting, followed by a subsequent meeting at the CFMEU, which resolved the issues.
Two CFMEU officials, Joe Myles and Paul Tzimas, attended the meeting along with four officials from the project, Young told the hearing.
Young said that while the commission had obtained significant documentation regarding the events leading up to the meeting, little was known about what occurred during it and why it was significant, so the commission would be reliant on the memory witnesses had of conversations four years ago.
The key questions included what stopped the work, and whether those disruptions were used as leverage by the CFMEU, he said.
It remained unclear exactly how much the CFMEU disruption to works on the site had cost, nor what the cost was to end the disruption, Young said.
But the union interrupted work on the site for 36 hours – and traffic controllers employed after the disruption charged significantly more than those previously employed, documents in evidence before the commission show.
The hourly rate increased from about $45 to $88, or from $59 to $147 for penalty rates, the documents show.
This meant, for example, that one 10-and-a-half hour shift cost $609 under the previous firm, but $1225 for the same shift under the new firm, Young said.
The Major Transport Infrastructure Authority director general started considering the cost implications of a CFMEU campaign to increase the rates of traffic controllers about the same time the disruptions occurred on the Gap Road project.
A September briefing prepared for the then minister for transport infrastructure, Jacinta Allan, estimated that the changes could cost the authority $60m to $78m for current projects, and well in excess of $400m for those projects in planning.
Royal commission that ‘Victorians deserve’
Earlier on Monday, the premier, Ben Carroll, said the royal commission was one “that Victoria needed and Victorians deserve”.
“I want every Victorian to get the answers they deserve,” Carroll said.
“This is a royal commission for Victoria. It’s a tough royal commission. It’s truly independent – [it has] the broadest terms of reference possible, a special prosecutor established as well. I said I’d do this in my first press conference and now it is up and running as it should be.”
Carroll confirmed legal representation for two former premiers, Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews, was “supported by the state” as has been the case at “other previous royal commissions”.
The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said: “They’ve trashed the future of this state, and now Ben Carroll is allowing the taxpayer to foot the bill for them to be defended in the royal commission, it doesn’t pass the pub test.”
The hearing continues.
– Additional reporting by Benita Kolovos

theguardian.com.title: Man accused of HungryPanda delivery rider’s stabbing murder yells and exposes himself in Melbourne court
theguardian.com.text:
A food delivery rider’s alleged murderer has pulled down his pants and exposed himself as he appeared in court.
Roberto Urbano, 51, appeared in Melbourne magistrates court via video link on Monday after being charged with murder and intentionally causing serious injury.
HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming, 47, and another rider confronted Urbano after spotting him tampering with their bikes in Melbourne’s city centre on Friday night, police allege.
After a fight broke out, Urbano allegedly stabbed both riders, with Feng dying at the scene.
The second rider, 34, suffered serious injuries and remained in hospital on Monday morning.
Appearing via video link, Urbano called out, “Objection, your honour!” before saying, “I’m the one who was injured”.
The video link was muted but he continued to speak and gesture with both hands and stood up to walk around multiple times.
He then stood on the chair and pulled down his pants exposing himself to the courtroom before the link was cut.
The magistrate granted the prosecution’s application to compel Urbano to have his injury to his right arm be photographed and his DNA extracted with a mouth swab.
His lawyer confirmed his client has schizophrenia and asked for the custody nurse to assess him.
The 51-year-old was arrested by police on Saturday and on Monday morning was charged with one count of murder and intentionally causing serious injury.
Investigators were granted extra time to build their case due to multiple witnesses requiring translators and more than 30 CCTV cameras needing to be canvassed, containing hundreds of hours of footage.
Feng, originally from China’s Shaanxi province, had been in Australia for about nine years.
His wife, Xu, both their parents and two children were all financially dependent on his work.
The news of Feng’s death reverberated through Melbourne and gig worker communities in Australia and abroad.
Mourners left floral tributes and notes near the state library over the weekend.
Some cards expressed sympathy for his family, while others vented grave frustrations with messages such as “city of criminal” and “Asian lives matter”.
A GoFundMe fundraiser set up by the Melbourne Chinatown Business Association had raised almost $390,000 by Monday morning to help Feng’s family with emergency travel and funeral expenses.
The head of the Melbourne Chinatown Business Association, Christina Zhao, said Feng’s death had weighed heavily on his colleagues and gig worker communities in China, Japan and Korea.
Food delivery company HungryPanda said it was assisting the family with visa arrangements, funeral expenses, financial support and insurance.
The Transport Workers’ Union said HungryPanda needed to confirm they properly assessed risks to their workers.
“HungryPanda has legal obligations to do whatever it can to minimise risk as food delivery riders carry out their work,” the national secretary, Michael Kaine, said on Monday.
“It must urgently confirm whether it has done this, and we are calling on WorkSafe to investigate whether it has failed in its duties here, as we have seen in the past with its failure to report a workplace death.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘Outrageous and racist’: premier responds to NSW One Nation candidate’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’
theguardian.com.text:
The New South Wales premier and the Australian Human Rights Commission have criticised comments by the man who heads One Nation’s upper house ticket in NSW after he said Australians faced demographic replacement unless “mass migration” was curtailed.
Chris Minns described Stuart Bonds’ comments as “frankly outrageous and racist”.
Minns said the replacement theory being espoused by Bonds was “just a conspiracy theory that’s been imported from the US here to Australia”.
Bonds will be the first candidate on the rightwing party’s NSW upper house ticket and on current polling is likely to be elected in March’s state election.
He made the incendiary remarks at an anti-immigration rally in Sydney’s CBD on Sunday. Several hundred people attended amid a sea of Australian flags.
At least one neo-Nazi, Joel Davis, was spotted among them, as well as rightwing figures including the national director of the Family First party, Lyle Shelton, who was previously head of the Australian Christian Lobby.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” Bonds told attendees after referring to abortion rates in Europe, the US and Australia.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we are going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”
He warned that unless it was stopped it would be “impossible to reverse”.
Bonds told the crowd that a country was “a shared culture, a shared border, a shared flag, a shared language and a dominant religion”.
“After 240 years, we are told we’re still on stolen land, and we’re meant to apologise for being here,” he said.
“Yet, in the same vein, we’re expected to believe that an immigrant arriving yesterday is as Australian as you and me. I don’t accept that people like the Bondi shooters are as Australian as you and me. I don’t accept that.”
The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said comments that some Australians were superior to others sowed “division and hate”.
“The idea that migrants can never truly be Australian ignores both our history and our shared future,” he said on Monday.
“Australia has always been shaped by successive generations of people who came here from around the world and helped build the nation we know today. It has the longest continuous culture in the world.
“Throughout history, periods of uncertainty have often seen minority communities cast as scapegoats. Today, migrants are too frequently portrayed as the cause of Australia’s challenges.
“Reducing complex problems to a simple narrative that migrants are to blame is not only inaccurate, it risks fuelling division, exclusion and racism. Migrants are not separate from the Australian story. They are central to it.”
Bonds told the rally that the “socialist plan” was to “destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation” pointing to European countries “on fire”.
He said Australia was going down a path “of becoming a special economic zone within Asia,” and that it needed to “re-establish ourselves as a proud Australian nation”.
Minns said voters should ask themselves which portfolio Bonds would have were One Nation to win the election.
“Trade, education, Treasury? I mean, what job will this bloke have in a Coalition-One Nation government?” Minns said.
“And are we going to see some distancing from those kind of views and those horrific perspectives or points of view from the Coalition?”
Comment was sought from the Coalition’s spokesperson on multiculturalism, Mark Coure, and from One Nation’s NSW headquarters.
Bonds’ comments were also reverberating in Canberra.
The federal minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, said Australians with migrant backgrounds were not replacing Australians – they simply were Australians.
“Questioning someone’s right to belong because of their race or ancestry is not a debate about immigration,” she said.
“It’s divisive, dangerous and goes against everything we stand for as Australians.”
– Additional reporting by Australian Associated Press

theguardian.com.title: Pope Leo delivers stinging rebuke of Milei’s austerity measures during Argentina visit
theguardian.com.text:
Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier Milei’s harsh austerity measures, insisting growth must benefit all in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.
“The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy,” he said on Sunday, shortly after landing in Argentina on the second leg of a Latin America tour.
Leo stressed the plight of those who, “despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household’s needs”.
He spoke out in defence of the poor and pensioners, insisting that “particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability” – a veiled reference to the government’s controversial cuts to disability assistance.
He also told Milei, known for his foul-mouthed diatribes, that strengthening democracy required a “willingness to listen” and the “careful use of words”.
Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 12-day tour of the continent, just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
The visit is the first by a pontiff to Argentina in nearly four decades, and Leo was met with calls to help mend deep divisions in the country after three years of austerity under Milei.
Argentina is the home country of the late pope, Francis, who Milei famously insulted for his pro-poor teachings.
Leo said he was “retracing” Francis’s steps.
Argentines are hoping the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics will help unite the country, which is bitterly divided between supporters and opponents of Milei.
“Just like the World Cup unites us, hopefully the pope will too,” said Liliana Deblauwe, a 68-year-old retired teacher who waited with hundreds of people to see the pope visit a monument to liberation hero Jose de San Martin.
Hundreds more chanting “Papa Leon” (Spanish for Leo) gathered outside the presidential palace, where he was hosted by Milei.
Brian Inacio Rodriguez, a 26-year-old job seeker, spent five days travelling overland from Ushuaia, at the very tip of South America, to see the pontiff.
He said he hoped he brought “much peace to Argentina”.
Leo arrived in Buenos Aires from Uruguay, where he began his first trip as pope to Latin America, the world’s most Catholic continent which is becoming increasingly secular.
In Uruguay, he condemned drug violence and urged an end to child poverty.
In Buenos Aires, he insisted on the importance of “personal integrity” in public office, stressing that “corruption undermines the confidence of citizens in their institutions.”
The Argentine stage of his visit aims to boost the flagging faith of a country left disappointed by Francis’s failure to visit during his papacy.
It will also act as a litmus test of support for the church. In a recent University of Buenos Aires poll, 57.7% of people identified as Catholic, down from about 90% in the 1960s.
Leo will visit a home for disabled people and a prison and celebrate three open-air masses.
The church has said it expects 7 million to attend the various events.
Milei came to office on a promise to revive Argentina’s ailing economy and tame runaway inflation by shrinking the welfare state, targeting public hospitals, universities and pensioners in particular.
The poverty rate has swung wildly since he came to power – increasing to 32.3% in September.
A close ally of US president Donald Trump, with a similar combative style, Milei had a tense relationship with Francis.
On the campaign trail the cost-cutting economist called his countryman an “imbecile” for championing social justice.
Once in office, however, he softened his tone, but he continues to heap insults on the press and opposition.
His relationship with Leo has so far been cordial, but the local Catholic church has heavily criticised him for treating key social services solely as a budgetary constraint.
Milei has also been criticised for restricting several democratic freedoms, including the right to protest. But he maintains a loyal supporter base for drastically reducing inflation.

theguardian.com.title: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making UFC’s Dana White next press secretary
theguardian.com.text:
Donald Trump said on Sunday that he “was only kidding” when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).
Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.
“So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump added. “Of course, I was kidding. And you could see that because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with him … It was just a little fun.”
Earlier on Sunday, the president shared an animated AI cartoon made by one of his supporters on social media, which showed UFC fighters beating up journalists and one, Josh Hokit, repeating the racist remark about Michelle Obama he made during the UFC event at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June.
The president said that his mock announcement that White would become his spokesperson, in a social media post on Saturday, “was an example of something where I was kidding, and then people said, ‘You know, that’s actually a pretty good idea’”.
He did not say who, exactly, supported the idea.
The first in a series of taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads broadcast by the White House in the run-up to the recent midterms closed with images of the UFC fight on Trump’s birthday and remarks about him from White, who could be heard saying: “He is the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life.” White used that formulation to describe Trump multiple times during the 2024 presidential election campaign, most notably to sing Trump’s praises at the Republican national convention.
The role of White House press secretary has been vacant for three weeks, since Trump’s previous pick, the far-right commentator Katie Zacharia, was forced to resign after trying, and failing, to dodge questions about why she described herself as an attorney despite having failed the bar exam.

theguardian.com.title: Maya Jama steps down as Love Island host after nine seasons
theguardian.com.text:
Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of Love Island after three years.
The 32-year-old presenter of the reality TV show made the announcement on Instagram.
Posting a highlights reel of herself on the programme, Jama said it was “time to throw myself into something new”.
“While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I’ll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever,” the TV and radio presenter said.
The move comes after Jama’s stint on the BBC’s Celebrity Traitors, as a traitor who breezed through the series undetected until the finale. Her popularity led to speculation in the Times that she could “get £1m per deal” thanks to her success.
Jama took over from Laura Whitmore as the host when the show returned for its ninth series early in 2023.
She was initially touted as a potential host after it was confirmed Caroline Flack would be stepping down as host in 2019, but the role was given to Whitmore.
Thanking fans and the production team on Love Island, she said she had an “unforgettable time” on the programme.
“I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the nine incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I’ve loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show.”
But she added: “I’ve always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then.”
An ITV spokesperson said: “Maya has been a fantastic and much-loved host on Love Island – we thank her for everything she has brought to the show over the last three years and wish her every continued success.”
Jama moved to London when she was aged 16 to pursue a career in the entertainment industry. She began her broadcasting work co-hosting Trending Live on 4Music and Cannonball on ITV, before moving to present her BBC Radio 1 show on Fridays and Saturdays.
At 23, she became the youngest person to co-host the Mobo awards on Channel 5 in 2017, alongside the JLS star turned presenter Marvin Humes.

theguardian.com.title: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
theguardian.com.text:
Nvidia said on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang said in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

theguardian.com.title: Two police officers hailed as heroes for confronting Kraków gunman
theguardian.com.text:
Two Polish police officers who were injured as they pursued and detained the gunman in Kraków on Saturday have been hailed as heroes.
One of them is Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, who was left critically injured after a close-range exchange of fire with the suspect, a 24-year-old Polish national who killed six and injured 17 in an attack believed to have been inspired by far-right ideologies.
The other injured police officer is Artur Morański. Both are under 30 years old, the Polish news network TVP World reported.
Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said on Saturday in a post on X: “They probably saved many human lives, disregarding the risk to their own.”
The Polish justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said the rapid response and heroism of the two police officers “prevented further human casualties”.
Police arrived at the scene 23 seconds after receiving the first emergency call from Kraków’s main square, where the suspect was shooting at random from his car.
Footage that emerged on Sunday showed two police officers exchanging fire with the gunman. One of the officers then apprehended the suspect on the ground before firing his own weapon several times. The officer then fell down, apparently injured himself.
Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, stepped in to help.
Wierdak “took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help”, Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet.
“Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.”
Kulik, from the southern Polish city of Bielsko-Biala, was hit by three bullets and underwent surgery on Saturday. There has been a national appeal for blood donors.
Morański was shot in the chest area and also underwent surgery. Both men were brought out of medically induced comas on Sunday, Polskie Radio 24 reported.
Kulik is also a member of the volunteer fire service in Bielsko-Biala. “We’re very proud of him,” a volunteer firefighter from the city’s Leszczyny district told the local news website Bielsko.biala.pl. “He responds to emergencies just like we do.”
TVP World reported that Morański was from Powroźnik, a village about 90 miles (150km) south-east of Krakow and close to the border with Slovakia. A mass was held for him at the local church on Sunday.

theguardian.com.title: ‘Seismic shift’: Native American women made significant gains in US midterms
theguardian.com.text:
The US midterm elections saw voters elect a slew of historic representatives – from the country’s first Muslim senator to the first Black female governor – but among the most significant gains were those for Native American women.
On Tuesday, voters elected the first Native American woman governor, senator and leaders of two tribal nations. Nationwide, voters elected at least 75 Native women or non-binary and Two Spirit candidates in the November midterms, according to Advance Native Political Leadership and the news site ICT.
Deb Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo and Joe Biden’s former interior secretary, will lead the state of New Mexico. Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe and current Minnesota lt governor, will represent her state in the US Senate. Crystalyne Curley will become the first woman to lead the Navajo Nation, one of the country’s largest tribes. And Tina Abrams will lead the Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York, also the first woman leader in the modern history of the state’s largest tribe.
Mary Peltola, who is Yup’ik, could join Flanagan as another first Native woman in the US Senate pending the results of her still undecided race in Alaska.
“This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities,” Jordan James Harvill, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation and strategist with Advance Native Political Leadership, told the Associated Press.
Although Native Americans have made significant gains in political power in recent years, it has been a long road to get here. Native Americans have only been allowed to vote across the entire United States since the 1960s. In 1985, Wilma Mankiller became the first woman elected to serve as principal chief of the Cherokee Nation.
In 2018, Haaland and Sharice Davids, a member of the Ho-Chunk Nation, became the first women elected to Congress when they both won seats in the House of Representatives alongside a wave of progressive freshmen lawmakers, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. Davids was easily re-elected last week in Kansas to a fifth term in Congress.
“The first thing that made [running for office] feel really possible was seeing Deb Haaland, was seeing Sharice Davids on a national level,” New Mexico state senator Angel Charley, who is Laguna/Zuni/Diné, told the Guardian about her decision to enter state politics in 2024.
In 2020, after an outpouring of voters from the Navajo and Hopi reservations in Arizona saw the long-red state vote for Biden, he named Haaland to lead the interior department, making her the first Indigenous cabinet secretary.
The same year, Yvette Herrell, who is Cherokee, became the first Republican Native woman elected to Congress. She served from 2021 to 2023.
This election cycle, a record-setting 363 Indigenous candidates ran for office in local, state and federal elections across the country – with at least 180 of them winning their races. Among them were Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo and Democrat from New York, who will join Davids in the US House of Representatives.
The Senate has seen four Native men represent their states in its 237 year history, but Flanagan will be the first Native woman to join the chamber in January.
At her victory party in St Paul, Minnesota, Flanagan told supporters: “I could not run for the US Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women.”
For Haaland, the historic nature of the election isn’t lost on her – but in the final weeks of a hectic campaign she told the Guardian that she sometimes forgets she’s on the verge of a milestone.
“Sometimes I forget about the fact that I would be the first Native woman. We’re in the throes of this statewide campaign and it’s so busy and we’re trying to be everywhere all at once,” she said in a recent interview. “But I recognize that for some people who feel like they haven’t ever been represented – I really, I’m grateful that I have this opportunity … I just hope that I can help folks to see that hard work still means something.
